We establish a general bound on this error for Lipschitz continuous functions, which depends on the trajectory of SGD. This bound comprises two components: one representing the excess risk of a fixed minimizer relative to the full dataset, and another quantifying the deviation of the partial-data SGD outputs from that minimizer. For Lipschitz continuous functions, we demonstrate that this deviation is influenced by the dataset size, the function's Lipschitz constant, and the SGD trajectory. Applying these findings to datasets with uniform distributions, we derive explicit bounds for neural network SGD outputs that converge to the global minimizer over increasingly larger data volumes. Additionally, for strongly convex functions, we prove that SGD trajectories approaching the minimizer result in deviations that decay exponentially with respect to the number of samples. These theoretical advancements are validated through experiments on deep neural networks trained on progressively larger subsets of MNIST and CIFAR-10 data. Our findings indicate that training on smaller data portions can still yield high accuracy, though with increased variance in the generalization error. Furthermore, we observe that SGD runs on smaller datasets exhibit greater sensitivity to initialization compared to those trained on larger datasets. These insights are particularly pertinent to scenarios where computational or memory constraints restrict access to the entire training dataset. Finally, our results suggest that employing a mini-batch size comparable to the batch used for the initial few steps enhances the robustness of SGD on smaller datasets. These conclusions are supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgarg123/SGD-on-increasing-size-of-dataset. This study examines a two-loop neural system characterized by two distinct loops within each loop, where connections between loops are achieved through electrical wiring. The primary objective is to analyze the synchronization of activity between the loop units. We demonstrate that activity synchronizes when the inter-loop coupling strength is sufficiently high, regardless of the specific coupling type. Furthermore, we establish that the relative phase of synchronized activity is consistently $\pi/2$. These dynamics were investigated using the Hodgkin–Huxley model, with numerical simulations supporting our theoretical findings. Additionally, we illustrate that synchrony can be maintained even when one loop exhibits significantly higher activity than the other. These results suggest that loop-loop synchrony in neural systems can be robustly achieved through electrical wiring. Finally, we highlight the potential application of our findings in the design of artificial neural systems. The theoretical insights presented herein may also offer valuable perspectives for developing brain-machine interfaces. This paper classifies the strong Gelfand pairs for the special linear groups SL(2, q). Additionally, we identify specific pairs (G,H) within semisimple algebraic groups where H is a Borel subgroup and all unipotent characters of H remain multiplicity-free when restricted to G. Our findings reveal that in most cases, these pairs constitute the complete list of strong Gelfand pairs involving a Borel subgroup. Furthermore, we observe that these multiplicity-free unipetal characters of H correspond to the characters of Weyl groups characterized by having a single non-zero Jordan block. This correspondence reveals a novel link between the representation theory of finite groups of Lie type and that of Weyl groups. The study of these pairs also yields insights into the geometry of symmetric spaces associated with real reductive groups. Specifically, the existence of a strong Gelfand pair (G,H) implies that the orbit closure of a symmetric space Kx under H is homeomorphic to a closed ball. To our knowledge, this research represents the first instance where symmetric spaces of a rank-one simple Lie group of exceptional type are linked to multiplicity-free phenomena. Finally, the classification of strong Gelfand pairs in this work enables the determination of all symmetric spaces whose orbit closures are homeomorphic to a closed ball within rank-one real reductive spaces. This list includes numerous previously unidentified spaces, thereby expanding the range of such geometries. The paper also incorporates an appendix that examines the relationship between strong Gelfand pairs and symmetric spaces whose orbit closures are homeomorphic to a closed ball. This study examines the 2:1 inner resonance within the TRAPPIST-1 system, focusing on systems where all three planets have comparable masses. We demonstrate that the resonant dynamics in a general three-body problem can be modeled as a Hamiltonian featuring a 1:1 resonance. By employing normal form theory, we derive an analytical expression for the Hamiltonian near the maximum, which takes the form of a quartet. This model successfully replicates the resonant behavior of the TRAPPIST-1 system. Furthermore, we establish that the quartet exhibits a global minimum at the origin and develops two additional critical points of the saddle type as parameters increase. These emergent saddle points generate a separatrix figure-eight shape, a feature that aligns with both numerical simulations and observational data. Finally, we analyze the stability of the resonant configuration in TRAPPIST-1 by investigating the evolution of the resonant argument and the Hamiltonian value. We determine that the system remains stable if the Hamiltonian stays below the level associated with the saddle points. Additionally, we estimate the timescale for resonant escape by modeling the evolution of the Hamiltonian as a random walk. Our findings indicate that the stability of the 2:1 inner resonance in TRAPPIST-1 is highly sensitive to the planets' masses. Specifically, the resonant configuration is unstable if the mass of the outer planet exceeds the middle planet by more than 20%, or if the middle planet is 20% heavier than the inner planet. These results offer valuable insights for future observations aimed at detecting resonances in other systems. Keywords: Resonances, TRAPPIST-1, Hamiltonian, Normal Form, Stability. The ILC is an energy-tunable electron-positron collider capable of accelerating beams to energies up to 500 GeV. This report outlines the detector's fundamental design, covering its overall concept, conceptual configuration, and performance projections. SiD is engineered to serve as a versatile instrument for both high-energy physics research and precise measurements in the Standard Model. It is optimised to achieve high-precision, high-luminosity data collection, while also delivering substantial sensitivity to astrophysical neutrinos. This collaboration is led by the SLAC Detector Group, a collective of institutions from California, Oregon, and Washington, and is supported by a European consortium comprising 13 universities and research centres. This study introduces a novel method for quantifying data quality in solar system contexts by analyzing the rate of change of the data. The algorithm was validated using Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF) data from the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) and the Advanced Space Environmental Monitor (AEM) on the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) and the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE). Furthermore, the study confirms that DQR values are consistent across different spacecraft, indicating that the technique is independent of specific instruments. Ultimately, this paper presents a new, straightforward, and reliable method for data quality assessment applicable to solar system observations. This approach can be extended to various heliospheric datasets, including those from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) and the Heliospheric Magnetic Connection (HMC) mission. This study introduces a reconfigurable architecture designed to accelerate the execution of decision trees and random forests. The proposed design integrates a pre-processor, a pre-order traversal engine, and a voting module, all implemented using partial very-large-scale integration field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). When tested on a Xilinx Artix-7 XC7ART250TG325C FPGA, the implementation achieved a maximum operating frequency of 200 MHz. Evaluations using the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (diagnostic) dataset demonstrated that the proposed design outperforms existing literature solutions in both training and classification accuracy. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with other state-of-the-art designs revealed that the proposed system offers superior accuracy and energy efficiency. Finally, the study provides a detailed comparison of hardware metrics—including area, power consumption, and frequency—against related works on decision trees and random forests. These results confirm the system's suitability for real-time applications, such as medical and defense diagnostics, where rapid and accurate classification is critical. The design is publicly available at https://github.com/Deepak-2000/Reconfigurable-architecture-for-decision-trees-and-random-forests.

This paper demonstrates that, for natural number functions with elementary computability, several properties are equivalent: being representable in the 1st-order theory of real exponentiation and being representable in the 1st-order theory of real multiplication. These representable functions encompass all elementary functions and more. Additionally, the study proves that the 1st-order theories of real exponentiation, real multiplication, and the real field are mutually interpretable. Furthermore, it is shown that the first-order theories of the standard natural numbers and the standard integers are mutually interpretable. These findings provide a novel, model-theoretic perspective on the relationship between the arithmetical theories PE and PA, which are 2nd-order counterparts to the exponentiated reals and exponentiated rationals, respectively. The paper also establishes that the theories of the standard natural numbers and standard integers are mutually interpretable with PE and PA. Finally, it is proven that the theories of the standard natural numbers and the standard reals are not mutually interpretable. These results offer a model-theoretic characterization of the relationship between PE and PA, which are widely recognized as the strongest known subtheories of Peano arithmetic. The findings align with a theorem by Wilkie stating that PA and its subtheories PE and PZF are not mutually interpretable. The conclusion of the paper discusses the implications of the obtained results in the context of Hilbert's 17th problem. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of dielectric loss mechanisms within transmon qubits, specifically focusing on the behavior of SiO2 and SiNx under microwave frequencies. To achieve this, we fabricated and characterized a series of resonators, including coplanar waveguide (CPW) and λ/4 types made from SiO2 and SiNx, integrated with transmon qubits. By measuring the unloaded quality factors of these resonators and the relaxation times of the transmons, we determined the specific dielectric loss tangent values for both materials. These experimental findings were compared against theoretical predictions derived from the bulk dielectric loss model. The resulting loss tangent coefficients are $\tan\delta_{CPW}=1.0(2)\times10^{-5}$ and $\tan\delta_{\lambda/4}=1.1(2)\times10^{-5}$ for SiO2, and $\tan\delta_{CPW}=1.4(2)\times10^{-5}$ and $\tan\delta_{\lambda/4}=1.5(2)\times10^{-5}$ for SiNx. Furthermore, the impact of these loss mechanisms on transmon relaxation times was examined. We observed that the transmon's contribution to the total dielectric loss is negligible compared to the coupled resonator. Consequently, the measured transmon contribution to the overall loss is an upper limit, with the actual bulk dielectric loss being higher. Finally, we evaluated how these bulk dielectric loss characteristics influence the performance of superconducting qubits in quantum computing applications. The findings indicate that the dielectric loss levels in sapphire-transmon systems are comparable to those in state-of-the-art silicon-transmon platforms. Additionally, the transmon's dielectric contribution to the loss is found to be insignificant, suggesting that the primary limitation for future transmon-based quantum processors will likely stem from packaging materials rather than the qubit fabrication process itself. This conclusion was also validated through an analysis of the coherence times of existing transmon qubits. Ultimately, these results suggest that the current bulk dielectric loss levels in silicon-transmon systems are not a limiting factor for the continued advancement of silicon-transmon quantum computing. The detailed fabrication and characterization procedures used to obtain these results are also provided. Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a powerful method for learning representations within graphs. This approach has proven particularly effective for identifying disease genes by leveraging the topology of biological networks. However, current GNNs typically treat all graph edges as equally significant, a simplification that overlooks the reality that edge weights often carry critical information. To address this limitation, we introduce a GNN framework that explicitly models the varying importance of edges. We applied this model to predict disease genes using the Human Gene Interaction Network (HGIN), a graph where edges represent gene interactions. Our results demonstrate that GNNs can effectively capture the disparity in edge importance, leading to a substantial improvement in gene prioritization performance. Furthermore, we validated that the learned edge weights align with established biological knowledge. These findings indicate that incorporating edge weight information enhances the accuracy of disease gene prediction. Consequently, this strategy holds promise for other GNN applications within graph-based biological networks. The source code for this model is available at: https://github.com/kuhara-lab/GNN-with-edge-weights.

This concept has recently been adapted to distributed complexity, where $n$ machines each hold a subset of a universe of size $m$. In this setting, the goal is to distinguish between two scenarios: either there exists an element absent from all machines' inputs, or every element appears in at least $k$ machines. Interior-point techniques offer rapid convergence but are limited to small-scale systems due to their high computational complexity. Conversely, first-order methods handle large-scale problems efficiently but suffer from slower convergence rates. This paper introduces a new hybrid strategy that merges both approaches to solve large-scale optimization tasks. The proposed algorithm begins with a coarse grid method to quickly achieve a near-optimal solution, followed by a multi-start conjugate gradient method to refine the result. Finally, a multi-start inexact Newton method further enhances the solution. This novel hybrid framework is demonstrated to outperform both interior-point and first-order methods individually across various performance metrics, including computational time, solution accuracy, and robustness. The efficacy of this approach is validated through its application to an optimal control problem in a large-scale chemical reactor. Additionally, the method is tested on a parameter estimation problem for a multi-unit power system, where it exhibits superior performance compared to standard interior-point and first-order optimization algorithms. This note investigates the post-critical dynamics of such maps, with a primary focus on those exhibiting a 2-to-1 degree. We demonstrate that, for almost all 2-to-1 bicritical rational maps, the post-critical set $P_c(f)$ is totally disconnected and contains a subset homeomorphic to a Poincaré disk that is invariant under $f$. Furthermore, we establish that the set of exceptional parameters—where $P_c(f)$ is connected—forms a set of Hausdorff dimension strictly less than 1 within the moduli space. These findings extend and complement the recently published work by Buff and Melian regarding quadratic rational maps with two critical points. Additionally, we identify a specific infinite collection of 2-to-1 bicritical rational maps where $P_c(f)$ is connected and characterize the local structure of this post-critical set. The dynamics associated with this family were previously analyzed by the second author in the context of parameter continuation. Our work also elucidates the parameter dynamics of this family by leveraging the existence of a real invariant line. To support the analysis of this data, we introduce a suite of Python modules designed to simulate the light curves of minor planets across various observational setups. The simulation process begins with a realistic generation of light curves, incorporating physical effects such as rotation, orbital motion, and libration, alongside stochastic variations caused by surface inhomogeneities. Finally, the simulated data is folded into a light curve file compatible with the lightcurve inversion code LightCurvePy. This workflow enables the testing of diverse analysis techniques on synthetic datasets, thereby providing a foundation for optimizing future analyses when new data becomes available. Additionally, the code facilitates the creation of artificial datasets for training machine learning models. We demonstrate this capability by applying the suite to a convolutional neural network for activity detection, showing that the model can be trained on simulated data and subsequently deployed to analyze real observations. Furthermore, we illustrate how the light curve simulator can aid in the inversion of activity models by generating data that covers a comprehensive parameter space. Finally, we provide a detailed comparison between simulated and real light curves to highlight the strengths and potential limitations of our code suite. We demonstrate that the Kac-Moody algebra, which governs the theory's operators, is influenced by the boundary condition at the curve. This algebra is generated by the holomorphic components of the energy and spin operators, which are constructed using fermionic fields arising from the Ising model's Ol'shanski Gelfand-Zetlin modules. Finally, we outline the procedure for deriving a non-local current algebra from the Virasoro algebra that accounts for these boundary conditions. This algebra is defined by a specific combination of the spin operator and the first component of the Ising field theory's energy-momentum tensor. Additionally, we identify a relationship between domain wall boundary conditions and the theory's partition function. This study examines the production of Z and W bosons through photon-photon fusion and their subsequent interactions with the hot, dense medium. We calculate the yield of Z bosons and their subsequent decays into neutrino-antineutrino pairs, observing that although production is suppressed relative to diphoton fusion, the resulting yield is substantial due to the high photon density. Furthermore, we investigate the potential for lepton number violation (LNV) mediated by LHC-scale LNV two-Higgs-doublet models, where a photon-photon LNV cross-section of up to 10 fb could be detected. We also analyze Z boson interactions with the medium, noting that while production is unaffected, the medium significantly influences lepton number distributions. Additionally, we explore the medium's impact on LNV, demonstrating that LNV lepton number can be amplified by as much as a factor of ten. Finally, we address lepton number violation arising from the asymmetric flow of leptons within the quark-gluon plasma. These findings suggest that diphoton-mediated electroweak lepton number production is a viable process, and the medium's effect on LNV lepton number distributions offers a unique signature for LNV physics at the LHC. Furthermore, the medium-induced amplification of LNV lepton number could serve as a critical test for the standard model in future colliders. This study investigates the long-term dynamics of the 1D Burgers equation within the slow diffusion limit, focusing on the emergence of shock waves. We demonstrate that these shocks develop within a specific time window that contracts to zero as the diffusion parameter diminishes. We evaluated this scheme using a trace-driven simulation framework, focusing on the IEEE 802.11p Physical Layer Convergence Protocol (PLCP) and Medium Access Control (MAC) layers. Our simulation results indicate that the proposed method can enhance packet delivery performance by up to 20% compared to traditional full or partial retransmission strategies. Furthermore, we developed a position-based packet success model to analyze the underlying mechanisms of these performance gains. This model serves as a valuable tool for predicting the packet success probability of IEEE 802.11p systems. Additionally, we examined the model's performance under various driving conditions, including different driving speeds, transmission ranges, and road segment lengths. Finally, we explored the model's applicability to IEEE 802.11p systems operating in different geographic regions, specifically comparing indoor versus outdoor environments and urban versus rural settings. These findings offer valuable insights for future research in vehicular ad hoc networks (VANETs). Furthermore, the proposed model can assist system designers in selecting appropriate transmission parameters and identifying optimal locations for transmitting critical information. It can also facilitate the analysis of packet success probability in IEEE 802.11p-based vehicular applications. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first study to analyze the impact of vehicle position on packet success probability within IEEE 802.11p-based VANETs. Our comprehensive analysis and extensive simulations provide strong evidence supporting the validity of the proposed model. However, existing methods often overlook the inherent non-stationarity of real-world systems, which can lead to inaccurate predictions. To address this, we introduce Non-stationary Lattice Boltzmann Prediction (NLBP), a novel framework designed for modeling non-stationary dynamical systems. Unlike traditional models, NLBP incorporates a non-stationary representation that adjusts model parameters dynamically based on the rate of change in the system. This non-stationary mechanism is realized through a generalized non-equation formulation of the lattice Boltzmann method, which offers both analytical and computational efficiency. We validated the effectiveness of NLBP by applying it to two non-stationary systems: the Lorenz system and the Japanese Yen/US Dollar exchange rate. Results demonstrate that NLBP outperforms established baselines, including the linear autoregressive model and the non-stationary recurrent neural network, in terms of prediction accuracy. Because HNLs interact primarily via weak forces, they can have lifetimes ranging from extremely brief to very long. This talk will focus on the search for long-lived HNLs, which remain largely unexplored by the LHC. We demonstrate that both 2D and 3D Gaussian ensembles of a fixed density $\eta$, along with Poisson processes, can be fully characterized by just two parameters: the dimensionless density $\eta$ and the parameter $v$, which represents the fraction of points within a distance of $1/\sqrt{\pi\eta}$ (or $1/\sqrt[3]{\pi\eta}$) from one another. For Gaussian ensembles, we derive an exact formula for $v$ as a function of $\eta$. Furthermore, we establish that ensemble inversion is feasible for both types, yielding a family of pair correlation functions $c_2(r)$ that are analytically invertible. This allows for the direct determination of void statistics for any given set of pair correlation functions. Finally, we examine the local structure of these ensembles by calculating the fraction of points enclosed within Delaunay cells and identifying the most probable cell volumes. Our findings indicate that points within small voids are more prevalent in the pair correlation functions of random close-packed spheres than in those of random dense packings. These results are validated through extensive numerical simulations. The proposed methodology for analyzing pair correlation functions is particularly valuable for comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data on disordered point sets. This approach is applicable to various systems, including colloidal monolayers, atomic and molecular liquids, granular materials, and other disordered point sets. The methodology was developed within the framework of the "Random Dense Packings" project, which investigates the pair correlation functions of randomly and systematically disordered disordered point sets. These functions are derived from the probability density function of the random packing process, enabling a direct link between microscopic details and macroscopic characteristics. This facilitates the analytical and numerical study of how ensemble properties evolve during the random packing of spheres and other particles. The project's outcomes are detailed in a series of publications, with a comprehensive review available in [1]. Additionally, an open-source software package, Pkg.PairCorr, has been created to assist in these analyses. This tool allows for the calculation of pair correlation functions, their inversion, and the computation of statistical properties of the local structure. The findings indicate that if $f$ exhibits sufficient decay at infinity, the INLS model is well-posed; however, the presence of such decay prevents the trivial solution. This study evaluates three audio-based accessibility solutions—Natural Reading (NR), Accessible Audio Description (AAD), and Accessible Audio Description for Books (AADB)—across four key criteria: reading speed, reading accuracy, reading experience, and content coverage. The research involved 16 participants who listened to the same books using each solution in a randomized order. Data analysis revealed that NR yielded the highest content coverage, followed by AAD and AADB. However, NR also resulted in the poorest reading experience and the lowest accuracy. Conversely, AAD achieved the highest accuracy but offered the least coverage. AADB provided a superior reading experience but had the lowest accuracy and coverage. These findings indicate that no single solution optimally addresses all four criteria. Additionally, the study found that participants' prior experience with specific solutions influenced their performance. Finally, the study successfully developed a dataset of 1,024 book excerpts featuring synthesized speech from NR, AAD, and AADB, which can assist future researchers in advancing audio accessibility technologies. This paper introduces a novel technique for generating supervised data for BERT-like pretraining by employing discriminative adversarial training. We term this approach "Adversarial BERT" (AdBert). By training BERT to resist adversarial noise, we demonstrate that AdBert surpasses standard BERT performance on NLP tasks where the input alphabet is limited, such as sentiment analysis. This study investigates how such gaps influence the chemical composition of the gas phase, with a specific focus on carbon monoxide (CO). We modeled a gap disk using the chemical code NAUTILUS, which solves the coupled chemical and thermal evolution of dust and gas under a one-dimensional vertical approximation. Our results indicate that the inner gap significantly suppresses CO production in the disk's midplane, primarily due to the destruction of gas-phase CO by oxygen atoms. These findings are robust across various gap sizes and disk aspect ratios. Consequently, the low CO abundances in the midplane of gap disks may complicate the detection of ongoing planet formation through millimeter-wave observations. Furthermore, our model predicts a substantial increase in solid-phase CO in the inner disk regions, a phenomenon that could be detectable by ALMA. Finally, we note that the inner midplane of these disks is rich in H$_2$O, a feature that could be verified using the MIRI instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope. In summary, the presence of an inner gap alters the CO inventory of the inner disk, shifting most CO from the gas phase to the solid phase. This has significant implications for interpreting millimeter-wave data and for the potential detection of inner disk H$_2$O via mid-infrared observations. These predictions can be tested using upcoming ground-based and space-based observatories. Our findings are supported by a comprehensive set of chemical models, with selected results presented in this paper. , are placed on a horizontal table and connected by a string passing over a pulley. The pulley itself has mass. Assuming the string is light and inextensible, determine the acceleration of the system. The setup is illustrated in the provided figure. Select the correct expression for the acceleration from the following options:

A. $\frac{m_1+m_2+m_p}{T}$

B. $\frac{m_1-m_2-m_p g}{m_1+m_2+m_p}$

C. $\frac{(m_1-m_2-m_p)g}{m_1+m_2+m_p}$

D. $\frac{(m_1+m_2+m_p)g}{m_1-m_2-m_p}$

**Correct Answer:** C

**Explanation:**

Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ represent the tensions in the string segments connected to masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, respectively. Applying Newton's second law to each mass yields:

$$m_1 g - T_1 = m_1 a$$
$$T_2 - m_2 g = m_2 a$$

For the pulley, the net force due to the difference in tensions equals the pulley's mass times its acceleration:

$$(T_2 - T_1) = m_p a$$

Summing these three equations eliminates the internal tensions:

$$m_1 g - m_2 g = (m_1 + m_2 + m_p) a$$

Solving for $a$ gives:

$$a = \frac{(m_1 - m_2 - m_p)g}{m_1 + m_2 + m_p}$$

Thus, option C is correct.

**Key Concepts:**

- **Acceleration:** The rate of change of velocity with respect to time.
- **Velocity:** The rate at which an object changes its position.
- **Displacement:** The change in an object's position.
- **Newton's Second Law:** States that the rate of change of momentum of a body equals the net external force applied to it.
- **Force:** The influence that changes the state of rest or uniform motion of a body.
- **Tension:** The force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable when pulled from opposite ends.
- **Mass:** The quantity of matter in a body, representing its inertia.

The analysis focuses on two scenarios: when the ultracold atom beam is polarized along the electric field axis and when it is unpolarized. In both cases, the primary contribution to the electric dipole moment arises from spin-orbit coupling, which transfers angular momentum from the electron spin to the nuclear spin. For the unpolarized sample, we demonstrate that the electric dipole moment can be enhanced by approximately a factor of 1.33 by preparing a sample with a nuclear spin quantum number of -1. These findings are expected to be applicable to other ultracold alkali atoms. Additionally, we have provided a concise analytical formula for the leading contribution to the interaction-induced electric dipole moment. This formula expresses the effect as a product of the square of the fine structure constant, the nuclear spin quantum number, and the motional contribution, which is equivalent to the expectation value of the reciprocal of the electronic kinetic energy operator. This motional contribution can be approximated using the expectation value of the reciprocal of the electronic potential energy, scaled by the electronic angular momentum. This relationship stems from a general property of the electronic wave function, where the electronic kinetic energy is distributed as evenly as possible. Furthermore, we have shown that the product of the interaction-induced electric dipole moment and the square of the electric field strength remains constant for a fixed nuclear spin quantum number, regardless of the specific values of the electronic angular momentum quantum numbers. This constant is determined by the expectation value of the reciprocal of the electronic potential energy. Finally, we have demonstrated that the product of the interaction-induced electric dipole moment and the square of the electric field strength can be approximately calculated using the expectation value of the reciprocal of the electronic mass. This product is found to be proportional to the square of the fine structure constant multiplied by the nuclear spin quantum number. These insights may prove useful for rapidly estimating the interaction-induced electric dipole moment in ultracold atoms. In summary, our results provide valuable insights into the microscopic origins of the interaction-induced electric dipole moment in ultracold atoms. While particle candidates like WIMPs have been extensively searched for without success, recent theoretical developments suggest that dark matter may instead consist of primordial black holes (PBHs). This study examines PBHs formed from the collapse of cosmic density fluctuations across a broad spectrum of masses. We demonstrate that the abundance of these PBHs is governed by the variance of density fluctuations, $\delta_\rho(k)$, integrated over a range of wavenumbers $k$. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula linking PBH formation to both the power spectrum of these fluctuations and the horizon size at the moment of collapse. This framework enables a more comprehensive analysis of how primordial black holes can account for dark matter. As an initial application, we show that PBHs with masses between $10^{-16}$ and $10^{-8}M_\odot$ could explain the recently observed excess in the Hubble constant ($H_0$) measurements from GRB 221009A. Additionally, we find that the recent LIGO/Virgo detection of a $3.2M_\odot$ black hole with a $0.14M_\odot$ companion might be interpreted as a binary system of primordial black holes. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of this research for the field of cosmology. The code used to calculate the abundance of PBHs is made publicly available. Additionally, we present a complete characterization of bounded smooth minimal $k$-harmonic functions under the same curvature conditions. These findings are derived from a more general theorem concerning smooth functions $f$ satisfying $\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{r}\|r\Delta f\|_{L^{p}_{M}}<\infty$ for $p\in[1,2)$, a condition that encompasses both harmonic functions and minimal functions. We also provide a complete classification of non-constant smooth minimal $\infty$-harmonic functions. Finally, we compare the behavior of $\infty$-harmonic functions under the assumptions of non-negative Ricci curvature versus non-negative scalar curvature. Our findings indicate that non-constant, smooth, bounded minimal $\infty$-harmonic functions exist under the non-negative scalar curvature assumption, whereas such functions are known to be constant under the non-negative Ricci curvature assumption. This distinction highlights the significantly weaker constraints imposed by the non-negative scalar curvature condition. Our results also provide a negative answer to a question raised by Wang. In this article, we utilize a generalized version of the Caccioppoli inequality, which may be of independent interest. Furthermore, we establish the existence of solutions to a class of Dirichlet problems for $k$-Laplace type equations, assuming a sign condition on the inhomogeneity. Galactic Nuclei (AGN) offers a means to investigate the magnetic field topology of the underlying engine. A critical method for this is the Faraday rotation of linearly polarized emission as it traverses the magnetized interstellar medium (ISM) of the host galaxy. While this technique has been applied to numerous sources, it remains underutilized for those exhibiting significant core and jet lobe hot bubbles. This work reports the first detection of Faraday rotation within the polarization of the linearly polarized emission from the large-scale jets of the radio galaxy NGC 1275. The measured Faraday depth for the jet is approximately 100 rad m$^{-2}$, with a corresponding uncertainty of roughly 10 rad m$^{-2}$. This finding is consistent with earlier observations of the jet's Faraday depth. The resulting Faraday depth is approximately ten times greater than the average values observed in the M81 group and the Perseus cluster. This elevated Faraday depth indicates a more turbulent magnetic field structure in NGC 1275's jets compared to other sources, likely due to the interaction of the jets with the hot gas surrounding the radio galaxy's core. Furthermore, the jets in NGC 1275 exhibit a more complex magnetic field structure than the regions within the radio galaxy's core. This suggests that the magnetic field topology is more intricate in the jets than in the core, a conclusion supported by the observed polarization patterns. Additionally, the study presents the first detection of circular polarization in the radio galaxy's core, with a measured value of approximately 10 microJy at 1400 MHz. This core circular polarization is roughly 100 times weaker than the circular polarization detected in the jets. Finally, the jets display a polarization fraction of about 10% at 1400 MHz, which is approximately 10 times lower than the polarization fraction in the core. This observation is consistent with the Faraday depth measurements and the general understanding of polarization in jets. These findings provide valuable insights into the polarization characteristics of jets in radio galaxies and their associated intracluster medium. We compute the canonical partition function and free energy for this system, accounting for boundary conditions and the quantization of electromagnetic modes. We demonstrate that the thermodynamic limit ($V \to \infty$, $\sigma \to 0$, with $Q$ constant) recovers the standard Stefan-Boltzmann law. Furthermore, we analyze the system's behavior under different constraints: when energy is fixed, we show that the entropy remains sub-extensive; when entropy is fixed, the internal energy is also sub-extensive; and when volume is fixed, both entropy and internal energy are sub-extensive. In each scenario, we derive the leading-order correction terms resulting from the cavity's finite conductivity. Additionally, we calculate the specific heat and radiation pressure, finding that specific heat fluctuations diverge as $\sigma \to 0$ when entropy or volume is held constant. Finally, we discuss the physical implications of these results. This study represents a preliminary investigation into black hole thermodynamics within an asymptotic AdS spacetime, framed as electromagnetic radiation trapped in a cavity of finite conductivity. It also serves as a foundational step toward investigating finite conductivity effects in black holes. The primary objective of this paper is to establish the theoretical framework for this investigation. Specifically, we derive the thermodynamic properties of radiation in a cavity with finite conductivity and examine the behavior of these properties in the limit where the cavity's size approaches the wavelength of the radiation. This limit is physically significant as it corresponds to the event horizon of a black hole. By understanding electromagnetic radiation in a cavity of finite conductivity, we can better comprehend the thermodynamics of a black hole. The findings of this paper provide a basis for future research on black hole thermodynamics. Specifically, we aim to investigate the thermodynamic properties of a black hole using the analogy with electromagnetic radiation in a cavity of finite conductivity. This will involve applying the finite conductivity framework developed in this study to a black hole scenario, thereby extending the investigation to a more complex physical system. Ultimately, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of the thermodynamics of black holes and their connection to electromagnetic radiation in a cavity of finite conductivity. The study of this relationship may provide insights into the fundamental nature of black holes and their thermodynamic properties. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. framework where all nodes interact by transmitting single-bit messages, known as beeps. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying a unique leader among $n$ nodes within such a network. We propose a randomized algorithm that achieves this identification with high probability in $O(n)$ expected time. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n)$ for both randomized and deterministic algorithms, demonstrating that no faster solution exists with high probability. Additionally, we examine the problem of determining $n$ using beep-based counters. Assuming nodes are equipped with these counters, we present a randomized algorithm requiring $O(\log^2 n)$ expected time. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the fastest known method for solving this problem in a single-hop beeping network. Finally, we provide a lower bound indicating that resolving this problem necessitates a minimum of $\Omega(\log n)$ beeps per node with high probability. All proposed algorithms operate without requiring any knowledge of network parameters. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm that enables $n$ nodes to synchronize their clocks with high probability in $O(\log n)$ expected time. This approach is the most efficient known for clock synchronization in single-hop beeping networks and relies solely on the assumption that each node possesses a unique identifier. We also demonstrate that this clock synchronization algorithm is essential for achieving the $O(\log^2 n)$ runtime for $n$-determination. Finally, we outline several open problems in the domain of single-hop beeping networks. These problems are significant because they encompass fundamental issues in distributed computing, such as leader election, $n$-determination, and clock synchronization. Solving them efficiently would substantially enhance the performance of distributed systems in resource-constrained environments. We introduce a variational upper bound on the KL divergence that depends on the approximating distribution as well as an auxiliary distribution from the same family. This bound is derived from the decomposition of the KL divergence into the information gain of the posterior relative to the approximating distribution plus the relative entropy between the auxiliary and approximating distributions. This decomposition facilitates the design of efficient update rules for both the auxiliary and approximating distributions. The proposed bound yields efficient inference approximations using a Gaussian mixture model with a fixed, small number of components, where each component corresponds to an approximate posterior. Additionally, the bound enables efficient estimation of continuous categorical distributions. These results are validated across various applications, including binary classification, regression, and density estimation. Our findings indicate that the bound performs competitively with other methods while requiring fewer parameters and fewer iterations to converge. Our approach decouples the control task into two distinct layers: a fast low-level layer that computes individual trajectories for each agent, and a slower high-level layer that generates reference trajectories to guide the low-level agents. We formulate the high-level control as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) and address the resulting combinatorial complexity by developing a novel dual decomposition algorithm. We provide a positive answer to this problem and further generalize it by demonstrating that the compactness requirement on the boundary can be relaxed to require only a finite number of compact components. Additionally, we investigate several related topics concerning the compactness of subsets and the compactness of points within the space. Finally, we examine a variant of the original question where the condition "every compact set has a compact neighborhood" is replaced with "there exists a coarser compactification for which the space is locally compact at each point." Both this variant and its converse have been recently resolved by E. Kakiuchida. Our work aims to explore certain related problems connected to these recent findings. Throughout this study, we employ various methods to construct counterexamples for several related questions. Notably, we establish multiple characterizations for the scenario in which a compact space $Q$ contains a dense subspace $X$ such that $X$ is locally compact at every point relative to the coarser topology induced by $X$ via the evaluation map. Our objective is to investigate this problem within the context of various other related questions. To our knowledge, this represents the first time the space $X$ is assumed to be first-countable diagonal, a property we demonstrate is essential for the space to be first-countable diagonal when viewed as a subspace of the Tychonoff cube. We also examine the case where the Tychonoff cube is replaced by an arbitrary compact Hausdorff space $K$, yielding a space $X$ with a compact-open evaluation map into $K$. We show that if $X$ is locally compact at each point, then $K$ is necessarily first-countable diagonal. Conversely, if $K$ is first-countable diagonal, we can construct a dense subspace of $K$ that is first-countable diagonal. a significant challenge, primarily because maintaining inter-robot safety distances is compromised by uncertainties in robot dynamics and sensor data. This study introduces a distributed model predictive control (MPC) framework for multi-robot navigation that incorporates safety filters to guarantee collision-free path planning. These filters are grounded in a geometric approach to collision avoidance, utilizing polytopes to represent robot states and ensuring a minimum separation distance. The proposed framework is validated through simulations involving 2D and 3D scenarios with various obstacle configurations. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the computational complexity associated with implementing safety filters for multi-robot navigation. The results demonstrate that the distributed MPC strategy successfully enables collision-free navigation for swarms of robots across 2D and 3D environments, even when navigating around obstacles and recovering from unsafe initial conditions. Additionally, the study confirms that the distributed MPC approach significantly reduces the time required to reach the target compared to methods that do not employ safety filters. Finally, the paper presents a detailed examination of the computational cost of implementing safety filters for multi-robot path planning. Numerical findings indicate that the most time-consuming component of the safety filter is the optimization problem solved at each time step to determine the safety margin. Crucially, this computational cost scales linearly with the number of robots, thereby facilitating the distributed implementation of safety filters in multi-robot navigation systems. Furthermore, the proposed distributed MPC algorithm is shown to be more computationally efficient than centralized MPC approaches for multi-robot path planning. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the distributed MPC method achieves comparable performance to centralized MPC while requiring substantially less computation time. Consequently, this research successfully integrates safety filters into multi-robot path planning, enabling collision-free navigation with reduced computational demands. However, recent observations reveal a significantly higher velocity dispersion than predicted by de Vaucouleurs models, suggesting a transition to a more complex structure. We present new data from the Arecibo Observatory, utilizing a sample of 120 pulsar candidates to establish a more accurate velocity dispersion. This updated value is substantially higher than earlier estimates, indicating that And XXV has evolved into an early-type galaxy with a de Vaucouleurs profile. Finally, we calculate the escape velocity and the number of pulsars required to measure the velocity dispersion at the escape velocity. These figures are notably greater than those for other dSph galaxies, implying that a larger number of pulsars would be needed to fully characterize And XXV's velocity dispersion. This paper introduces a novel and unified framework for modeling grant-free access in 5G and beyond cellular networks, specifically targeting scenarios with high user density and limited reference signals. The study addresses two core challenges: 1) the design of grant-free protocols and 2) the development of detection algorithms. To facilitate this, we establish a unified framework for massive multiple access schemes, enabling the performance characterization of various user-centric and group-sparsity algorithms under high user density and minimal reference signal constraints. Leveraging this model, we derive closed-form expressions for key metrics including outage probability, average delay, and average distortion. Additionally, we propose and evaluate multiple detection algorithms, assessing their strengths and weaknesses through numerical simulations. Our findings indicate that the proposed framework and performance metrics are applicable to broader contexts, such as group-based grant-free access involving massive user counts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the average distortion metric effectively captures the trade-off between distortion and outage, highlighting its utility for group-based grant-free access systems. This research offers valuable insights for future protocol design and detection algorithm development. The paper is structured as follows: Section II introduces the system model and the unified grant-free protocol modeling framework; Section III details the performance of user-centric algorithms; Section IV examines group-sparsity algorithms; and Section V presents numerical results. Finally, Section VI provides concluding remarks. This study investigates the stability of these PTS solitons within a confined CPTA reaction medium using a stability matrix analysis. The findings indicate that the PTS structures are unstable, exhibiting decay over time. These results are supported by experiments utilizing a confined CPTA reaction mixture, which demonstrates that the observed patterns are intrinsic to the reaction-diffusion system itself. The instability arises from an eigenvalue of the stability matrix possessing a positive real part, a condition that is independent of the specific boundary conditions applied to the system. Consequently, it is concluded that palm tree solitons are inherently unstable in the CPTA reaction-diffusion system. This stability matrix analysis offers a general approach for determining the stability of localized patterns in reaction-diffusion systems. Furthermore, the study suggests that the previously reported stability of palm tree solitons in the confined CPTA reaction medium was an artifact of the experimental setup. Finally, it is argued that the observed decay of palm tree solitons in confined CPTA reaction media is likely attributable to the evaporation of water from the reaction mixture. These conclusions are consistent with the observation that palm tree solitons remain stable in the CPTA reaction-diffusion system when confined within a hydrophobic container. The stability matrix analysis can be applied to other systems exhibiting localized patterns to determine their stability. Additionally, the analysis suggests that the stability of these patterns is governed by the properties of the reaction-diffusion system itself, rather than the boundary conditions imposed on it. This insight may assist in designing experiments to observe stable localized patterns in reaction-diffusion systems. We frame SGD as a constrained optimization problem and develop a flexible regularization method that approximates the SGD solution under a given step size and iteration count. This approach yields a new regularized least squares estimator, which we term the Regularized SGD (RSGD) estimator. We demonstrate that RSGD serves as a smooth and continuous extension of SGD, offering a pathway to analyze SGD solution properties through the lens of regularization. Furthermore, we establish that RSGD shares the same minimizers as SGD, and under standard assumptions, it achieves the optimal convergence rate for least squares problems with minimal bias. Additionally, we prove that RSGD is statistically equivalent to SGD under a local strong convexity condition. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of RSGD through numerical experiments. Our findings indicate that RSGD serves as a useful tool for interpreting SGD, particularly in scenarios involving large step sizes and limited iterations. In these contexts, RSGD uncovers insights into the relationship between SGD behavior and underlying data characteristics, such as dimensionality, sparsity, and low-rank structure. Notably, in cases where SGD exhibits high bias, RSGD can surpass SGD in predictive performance. These results are derived from extensive numerical experiments across various datasets. We demonstrate that RSGD excels on high-dimensional sparse data, effectively acting as a continuous analogue of Lasso. Conversely, on low-dimensional data where SGD is already highly accurate, RSGD performs comparably to SGD. These outcomes align with existing theoretical predictions. Overall, our study indicates that the RSGD estimator holds significant potential for enhancing the interpretability of SGD. By elucidating the link between regularization and iterative methods, we aim to foster a deeper understanding of SGD and its application across diverse fields. a one-dimensional Bose gas composed of $N$ particles confined within a box of length $L$ and interacting via a $\delta$-repulsion of strength $\gamma$. We demonstrate that, for large $N$ and a mesoscopic scale $\lambda = N/L$ (where $N \gg \lambda \gg 1$), the time evolution of occupation numbers can be accurately approximated by a non-linear Schrödinger equation with a $\delta$-potential. Furthermore, we establish that the dynamics of this equation are well-approximated by those of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation (CNLE) up to a time scale of $O(\lambda^2)$. To validate these findings, we present numerical simulations for the occupation numbers of the Bose gas, which show excellent agreement with both the CNLE and the $\delta$-modified version of the CNLE. Finally, we extend these results to systems with periodic boundary conditions. Our methodology is applicable to any $\delta$-interaction, whether attractive or repulsive, and holds significant physical relevance, particularly for understanding dynamics in one-dimensional systems exhibiting integrability. Additionally, the results may be tested experimentally using ultracold atoms in optical lattices. The study begins with an analysis of the many-body Schrödinger equation for the Bose gas, followed by a discussion of the $\delta$-non-linear Schrödinger equation and its relation to the CNLE. We then examine the approximation error, which is $O(\lambda^{-1})$, and conclude with a discussion of the findings. This work constitutes the second part of a two-article series; the first part, which provides a general framework for deriving non-linear Schrödinger equations from the many-body Schrödinger equation, is available on arXiv at arXiv:1903.01220. In this second part, we specifically address the $\delta$-interaction case. In this context, the derived non-linear Schrödinger equation corresponds to the $\delta$-CNLE, a model previously analyzed in the literature. We first prove the existence and uniqueness of its solution, then compare the CNLE with the $\delta$-CNLE, highlighting the significant impact of the $\delta$-potential on the dynamics. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the physical system under consideration. However, its performance in estimating the $L_\infty$ norm is highly sensitive to the choice of hash functions, a limitation that has historically hindered its practical application. This work introduces a novel CountSketch variant that recovers the exact value of the $L_\infty$ norm with high probability. The memory efficiency of this new approach is comparable to the best existing constant approximation algorithms. Furthermore, the algorithm is straightforward to implement and executes quickly. Finally, we present empirical results demonstrating the method's efficacy. To our knowledge, this is the first CountSketch-based algorithm capable of exactly recovering the $L_\infty$ norm with high probability. Additionally, we provide a positive answer to an open question regarding the memory complexity of exact $L_\infty$ norm recovery in data streams. These results are derived from a deeper theoretical analysis of CountSketch, which may hold independent significance. Specifically, we demonstrate that the success of our algorithm stems from a previously overlooked property of random linear projections on vectors with sparse supports. This insight may facilitate the exact recovery of other types of structured vectors using linear sketches. Our proofs are rigorous, employing a non-asymptotic analysis of the error distribution of CountSketch that avoids reliance on asymptotic assumptions. This approach may also enable precise error estimation for other linear sketching algorithms. Furthermore, our findings offer a new perspective on the success of linear sketches, shifting the focus from randomization within individual entries to randomization applied to the entire vector. This vector-level randomization has the potential to yield more accurate estimates with fewer sketches. Finally, we present a new algorithm that exactly recovers the $L_\infty$ norm using less memory than any existing randomized algorithm. This achievement is made possible by our novel perspective on vector recovery, which allows us to leverage the strengths of both linear and non-linear techniques. ### 1. Introduction

Personalization is a critical factor in the success of numerous machine learning applications. For instance, in online news platforms, content is tailored to individual users, and in recommendation systems, models are typically trained and maintained per user. However, when a model is trained for a specific user, it is often difficult to determine whether its performance will degrade as that user's preferences shift. Conversely, when dealing with many users, it is often more efficient to train a single policy that generalizes across a population rather than training separate models for each individual.

This paper focuses on the challenge of adapting to dynamic user preferences. We begin by examining existing approaches for personalized policy learning and their inherent limitations. We then present a simple yet effective method for meta-learning dynamic user preferences. This approach involves training a meta-policy on examples of policies that have already been customized for individual users. We demonstrate that this meta-policy can generalize to new users and evaluate its performance against several state-of-the-art personalization methods. Our results indicate that the meta-policy achieves competitive performance compared to these state-of-the-art methods.

Our findings indicate that entrainment is reciprocal, with speakers mirroring each other's voice pitch, intensity, and speech rate. We find that the final-state elliptic flow $v_2$ is highly sensitive to the equation of state (EoS) governing the matter evolution phase. Specifically, employing a soft EoS results in a significantly reduced $v_2$ compared to a stiff EoS. This sensitivity arises because the soft EoS suppresses the pressure anisotropy required to generate elliptic flow during the collision's early stages. Furthermore, we observe that the ratio of $v_2$ to initial spatial eccentricity remains greater than one in the final state, indicating that geometric initial conditions are a primary driver of final-state elliptic flow. Finally, we explore the impact of parton mean free path on $v_2$ and its dependence on collision energy. Our findings suggest that a longer parton mean free path diminishes the sensitivity of $v_2$ to the EoS. These results are analyzed through the lens of parton mean free path and the number of participants. Additionally, we investigate the effect of parton mean free path on the ratio of $v_2$ to initial spatial eccentricity. We conclude that a larger parton mean free path increases this ratio, suggesting that anisotropic flow is more pronounced when parton interactions are weaker. These conclusions are derived from comparing the calculated ratios for the two specified collision systems. Our study demonstrates that $v_2$ serves as a valuable tool for investigating the equation of state in heavy-ion collisions. The results demonstrate that, under certain conditions, the system's long-term dynamics are significantly influenced by the initial conditions within the phase plane. Specifically, the system possesses at most four boundary equilibrium points, and the local asymptotic stability of each is determined based on the local diffusion coefficient $D$. Furthermore, we establish that the system does not support Hopf bifurcations or chaotic dynamics within the phase plane. Finally, the local dynamics are explored through a comparison of two representative cases: one with a small $D$ and another with a large $D$. Additionally, the global dynamics are analyzed using the average first passage time (AFPT) and the stationary distribution derived from it. Numerical simulations illustrate that, for a fixed $D$, varying the initial conditions can result in different AFPTs and stationary distributions. These findings are further demonstrated through a series of representative examples. Ultimately, the study concludes that both local and global dynamics are heavily dependent on the local diffusion coefficient $D$. This research contributes to the broader field of nonequilibrium statistical physics by highlighting the critical role of local diffusion in shaping system dynamics. Furthermore, it offers insights into the local dynamics of real-world predator-prey systems, which are frequently influenced by the local diffusion coefficient. we investigate the relationship between the properties that every finitely generated left $R$-module possesses either uniserial quotients or uniserial submodules. Let $P_1$ denote the property where each finitely generated module has only uniserial quotients, and let $P_2$ denote the property where each finitely generated module has only uniserial submodules. It is established that if $R$ is right Noetherian, $P_1$ holds if and only if $R$ is right serial; similarly, if $R$ is left Noetherian, $P_1$ holds if and only if $R$ is left serial. We demonstrate that $P_1$ implies $P_2$, yet provide counterexamples to the converse. Specifically, we construct right Noetherian rings where $P_2$ holds but seriality does not. Conversely, for any non-zero integer $n$, we give an example of a right Noetherian ring $R$ where the module $R^2 \oplus R^n$ fails to be serial, thereby showing that $R$ is not right serial and $P_1$ does not hold. Additionally, we present examples of rings that are not right Noetherian, where $P_2$ holds but $R$ is not right serial. Finally, we present examples of rings where neither $P_1$ nor $P_2$ is satisfied.

Our findings indicate that EVBA accurately predicts the differential and integrated cross sections for VBF processes in the transverse polarization limit. However, we observe a substantial discrepancy in the nonperturbative region of the rapidity difference between the two leading jets. We recommend that current experimental limits, which constrain the Standard Model (SM) Higgs cross section using VBF data, should be re-evaluated using a full off-shell calculation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the EVBA remains valid for non-SM scenarios, such as models with anomalous couplings. Finally, we illustrate that including additional SM contributions, specifically top-loop effects, can resolve the discrepancy between the VBF and jet+tagging distributions. These results suggest that the apparent excess in the transverse rapidity distribution reported by the CMS collaboration in their 125 GeV SM Higgs cross-section measurement may stem from the use of an effective calculation rather than a full off-shell computation. Additionally, we show that the EVBA can serve as a sensitive tool for detecting new physics in the nonperturbative region. Given that VBF data are currently among the most precise measurements of the SM Higgs cross section, our analysis underscores the need for more accurate theoretical predictions. We conclude by presenting the first complete off-shell prediction for VBF processes. This prediction establishes a baseline for interpreting upcoming VBF data and may reveal new physics in the high-$|y_{\Delta\eta}^{jj}|$ region. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the recently proposed "double-tag" method for measuring the SM Higgs cross section is viable within the SM. We also examine the sensitivity of the VBF process to new physics, showing that the cross section can be enhanced by a factor of 10 through anomalous couplings, while remaining consistent with existing constraints. Finally, we show that a significant fraction of the cross-section enhancement can be achieved through interference effects. Overall, these results suggest that the VBF process holds promise for discovering new physics at the LHC. 16-BLG-1010 was identified through the OGLE-IV survey, featuring a planet with a mass of 0.14 Earth masses orbiting at 1.92 AU. This discovery was achieved by combining data from microlensing planet-finding initiatives, including KMTNet, MOA, and OGLE. The identification relied on analyzing the caustic crossing phase of the signal, which enabled a precise determination of the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$). By applying the Einstein ring radius ($R_E$) method, the system's total mass was derived. This study details the analysis of OGLE-2016-BLG-1010 and its role in the ongoing effort to identify super-Earth and sub-Jupiter mass planets. Additionally, the paper outlines the OGLE-IV survey's contribution to planet detection, the methodology for identifying the signal, and the specific analysis techniques employed. The analysis utilized a joint fit of KMTNet and OGLE data, while the KMTNet dataset was further divided into three subsets based on the observing sites of SAAO, AASTRO, and NUSTAR. The OGLE dataset was processed using the MACHO pipeline, and the final model was determined by comparing the joint fit results with the MACHO analysis. The resulting light curve analysis confirmed the presence of a low-mass planet, with the KMTNet data providing the critical information necessary for this detection. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the entire analysis process, from raw data collection to the final identification of the planetary system. The joint fit yielded a planet-to-star mass ratio of $q = 2.63 \pm 0.11 \times 10^{-7}$ and a relative Einstein radius of $R_{RE} = 0.94 \pm 0.06$ mas. Applying the $R_{RE}$ method to these parameters resulted in a total system mass of $M = 0.53 \pm 0.09 M_{\odot}$. This analysis demonstrates that the OGLE-IV survey, in conjunction with KMTNet, is highly effective at detecting low-mass planets. Furthermore, the paper discusses the advantages of using a joint fit, which significantly reduces the uncertainty in the mass ratio. Finally, the study concludes with an analysis of the planet's characteristics and its position within the habitable zone. The OGLE-IV survey continues to be a vital tool

### 1. Introduction
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently gained significant traction due to their ability to effectively model node relationships within graphs. However, despite their proven success, GNNs remain vulnerable to attacks. Previous studies have explored various strategies to disrupt these networks, including removing nodes, altering node features, and linking nodes to a malicious graph. In this work, we propose a new and efficient method for generating a minimal set of clean nodes that, upon connection to a malicious graph, can successfully deceive GNNs. We evaluate our method against two distinct objectives: (1) deceiving the network by creating a compact set of edges that results in graph structures indistinguishable from the original, and (2) deceiving centrality metrics by linking a specific node to a malicious graph. Our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in both scenarios. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/pg-link.

This paper introduces a novel consensus mechanism termed "Plasma," which leverages the inherent asynchronous nature of distributed systems to achieve linearizability. Unlike many contemporary consensus protocols, Plasma does not impose specific constraints on message scheduling or distribution. Furthermore, it avoids the need for an additional layer of primitive agreement, such as leader election, to ensure its correctness. By applying the Bohm-Holevo interpretation to the system's wave function, we reveal a tension between two principles: (i) the non-increasing of mutual information between a pair of systems during unitary evolution, and (ii) the ability to perfectly identify which path a particle takes when the interferometer is sufficiently isolated. We argue that to maintain the first principle, the second principle must be abandoned. This conclusion leads to the irretrievable loss of the "recoil" effect within the explanation. Furthermore, this result implies that the wave function of the total system cannot be meaningfully partitioned into subsets corresponding to individual components, a step essential for the von Neumann measurement scheme. Ultimately, these findings indicate that the Bohm-Holevo interpretation struggles to explain the quantum measurement process in this specific system. The source of this difficulty lies in the non-local correlations inherent in the unitary evolution of the total system, which are crucial for accounting for the experimental outcome. We contend that these non-local correlations are incompatible with the localized space-time framework of the Bohm-Holevo interpretation. Consequently, we propose that the von Neumann measurement process in this system should instead be elucidated using the standard Copenhagen interpretation. This approach offers a more comprehensive and satisfactory explanation of the quantum measurement process in the system, including the quantum erasure and recoil paradox, compared to the Bohm-Holevo interpretation. Additionally, we discuss the significance of the quantum erasure and recoil paradox within the broader context of the development of quantum mechanics. We examine the relationship between the non-locality of the wave function in the Bohm-Holevo interpretation and Bell's theorem, addressing the apparent conflict between the single-valuedness of the Bohmian trajectory and the non-local correlations present in the wave function. We also address the issue of the non-deterministic nature of the measurement outcome in the Bohm-Holevo interpretation, contrasting it with the deterministic evolution of the wave function. Finally, we address the challenge of explaining macroscopic distinctness in measurement using the wave function, a difficulty that the Copenhagen interpretation avoids. We further explore the relationship between the wave function and the detector in the Copenhagen interpretation, demonstrating that the detector's initial state can be decomposed into orthogonal subspaces representing different measurement outcomes. We show that the reduced density matrix of the detector, derived from the unitary evolution of the detector and system, can be diagonalized into a form where each diagonal element corresponds to a specific measurement outcome. This study examines the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the nearby galaxy M81, which exhibits a flat spectrum with a spectral index of approximately 0.5 across the 100 MeV to 100 GeV range observed by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). We demonstrate that the gamma-ray emission from M81 can be adequately explained by the inverse Compton scattering of electrons with the intra-galactic medium, cosmic microwave background, and starlight, as well as by inverse Compton radiation from electrons accelerated at pulsar wind nebulae and supernova remnants. Furthermore, we find that the gamma-ray flux from CRAND is negligible for M81. The flat spectral shape is best replicated by a population of electrons with a power-law distribution in energy, which aligns with the electron population located in the galaxy's disk. This suggests that gamma rays from M81 originate from electron interactions with photons from the intra-galactic medium, cosmic microwave background, and stars, rather than from hadronic interactions. Consequently, the gamma-ray spectrum of M81 provides strong evidence for flat electron spectra in disk galaxies. This study investigates the relationship between a model's ability to learn complex functions and its expressiveness within the NTK regime. We introduce a novel framework to analyze the spectral characteristics of the inner product matrix across various data distributions, thereby establishing a link between this matrix's spectral properties and the model's expressivity. Furthermore, we define and examine the concept of "spectral expressivity," which depends on both the spectral features of this inner product matrix and the spectral dynamics of the Riemann-zeta function. Our findings indicate that the spectral expression of data serves as an upper limit for the model's standard expressivity. Additionally, we explore how spectral expressivity evolves with increasing model dimensions and depth, observing that it diminishes as dimensions expand but rises with greater depth. # Introduction

Data is fundamental to the success of machine learning models, particularly in the realm of recommendation systems. These systems rely on user interactions to deliver personalized experiences. However, the requirement for large volumes of private data creates significant hurdles for data sharing, especially for organizations seeking to develop collaborative models. While various techniques exist to protect data privacy, they often degrade model performance. This paper addresses the challenge of sharing data while maintaining privacy and minimizing performance degradation. We propose a solution that facilitates the sharing of data-driven user profiles for recommendation tasks by blending them with synthetic data. This approach allows organizations to share synthetic versions of user profiles, thereby enhancing personalized recommendation models.

We begin by outlining a method for generating user profiles and a technique for creating synthetic data. Subsequently, we present a scheme for sharing these synthetic profiles to improve the User-side and Model-side components of a recommendation system. Our approach involves mixing user data with synthetic data to form synthetic profiles, which are then utilized in both the user and model phases of the recommendation

traditionally focused on planets orbiting main-sequence stars, the growing number of exoplanets around white dwarfs (WDs) and white dwarf binaries (WDBs) offers a unique opportunity to investigate planet formation and survival across stellar evolution. This review examines the demographics of these systems, their formation mechanisms, and the history of their planetary systems. We highlight the significant challenges posed by the current lack of data on planets in WDs/WDBs compared to those in main-sequence stars, and we identify key observational and theoretical uncertainties that must be resolved to advance the field. Our primary conclusion is that the current sample of exoplanets in WDs/WDBs is too small to draw definitive generalizations, yet it already reveals that the surviving planets are likely a biased subset of the original population. Furthermore, we emphasize the need for a more diverse array of host stars, particularly WDs with masses below 0.6 solar masses, to better understand the full scope of planetary systems throughout stellar evolution. Finally, we outline a strategy for future research, including the application of high-precision astrometry to detect low-mass planets in these systems. We conclude that the emerging field of planetary systems around WDs/WDBs holds great promise for uncovering novel insights into planet formation and evolution. Our approach employs a Monte Carlo simulation of the LW photon spectrum, utilizing a self-consistent model of the Ly$\alpha$ background derived from an analytical solution to the source-free transfer equation. This solution is valid for homogeneous sources and absorbers and applies to redshifts $z\lesssim 10^3$. Our findings indicate that excitation and ionization by LW photons are negligible at all epochs, even when the Ly$\alpha$ background is fully saturated. Consequently, the thermal radiation field remains the primary driver of hydrogen excitation and ionization throughout the early universe. This result holds significant implications for the physics of the cosmic dark ages and the subsequent formation of the first stars. Furthermore, LW photons are the sole agents responsible for the (de-)excitation of hydrogen atoms in the intergalactic medium (IGM) at redshifts $z\gtrsim 2.5$, where the Ly$\alpha$ background is not saturated. We also explore the potential for LW photons to induce hydrogen recombination in the IGM, though this process is far too slow to account for the rapid recombination observed in the early universe. Finally, we examine the impact of LW photons on the ionization of helium in the IGM. We conclude that LW photons are the dominant source of helium ionization for $z\gtrsim 10^3$, whereas thermal radiation takes over at lower redshifts. This early ionization of helium may have critical consequences for the formation of the first stars. Additionally, LW photons are the sole source of ionization for helium in the early IGM, and their contribution is substantial at $z\sim 10^3$. This suggests that LW photons could play a pivotal role in the evolution of the IGM and the formation of the first stars. We also investigate the effect of LW photons on the formation of molecular hydrogen in the IGM. Our results show that LW photons can destroy molecular hydrogen at $z\gtrsim 10^3$, potentially hindering the formation of the first stars. However, LW photons are ineffective at destroying molecular hydrogen at redshifts $z\lesssim 10^3$.
