This study investigates the electronic properties of Cr$_2$Al under external pressure using first-principles calculations. We find that increasing pressure causes the Fermi level to shift toward the valence band, thereby intensifying the Weyl points. Specifically, the type-Q Weyl points located at the X and K points in the Brillouin zone move deeper into the valence band, while those at the L point shift toward the conduction band. At a pressure of 10 GPa, the type-Q Weyl points at the X and K points touch the valence band edge, causing the material to transition into a zero-gap semiconductor. This semiconductor features Dirac points at both the X and K points within the first Brillouin zone. Furthermore, applying 20 GPa of pressure induces a semiconductor-to-metal phase transition. These findings suggest that applying external pressure offers a viable method for achieving a zero-gap semiconductor phase in Cr$_2$Al. Additionally, we calculated the anisotropic magnetotransport characteristics of this zero-gap semiconductor phase. The calculated magnetotransport behavior aligns with the electronic structure characteristics typical of zero-gap semiconductors. Consequently, Cr$_2$Al is anticipated to exhibit an extremely large magnetoresistance under external pressure. This research expands the family of zero-gap semiconductors and provides a new perspective for discovering materials with giant magnetoresistance. Finally, we recommend exploring Cr$_2$Al for applications in spintronics and magnetoresistance devices. The calculated zero-gap semiconductor phase in Cr$_2$Al is comparable to that in Cd$_3$As$_4$, another well-known zero-gap semiconductor. This comparison underscores the potential of Cr$_2$Al as a promising candidate for future electronic devices. Furthermore, Cr$_2$Al may serve as a new model system for investigating the quantum critical point between zero-gap semiconductors and metals. These theoretical predictions warrant experimental verification. Such experiments would not only validate the predicted zero-gap semiconductor phase in Cr$_2$Al but also advance the broader field of quantum materials. In summary, this work broadens the scope of materials exhibiting giant magnetoresistance and offers a fresh avenue for the discovery of such materials. While some theories suggest QPOs may arise from the inner accretion disk, the corona, or the jet, this study proposes that they originate in the accretion disk itself, specifically within the magnetized boundary layer connecting the disk to the stellar surface. By applying the global magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model previously developed for ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs) to X-ray pulsars (XRP), we demonstrate that this boundary layer generates QPOs with periods matching those observed in both XRP and ULX sources. The model attributes these oscillations to the standing kink mode of the magnetic field in the boundary layer. Furthermore, we show that the amplitude of the kink oscillation scales with the magnetic field strength in the boundary layer, which can be estimated using the magnetic flux accretion rate. This paper presents the initial findings of our global MHD global model applied to XRP, with future work focusing on comparing our results to actual X-ray data. We anticipate that this model will provide valuable insights into the nature of QPOs in XRP. Additionally, we have previously demonstrated that this same global MHD model successfully explains the bolometric luminosity of ULX sources. Consequently, we conclude that the boundary layer in ULXs is a critical component of their overall structure. We demonstrate that for any finite set $\mathcal{F}$ of multivariate monomials, these polynomials, when restricted to $\mathcal{F}$, coincide exactly with the Legendre polynomial $P_{\mathcal{F}}$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^m$ associated with the uniform discrete measure supported on the vertices of the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$. mode-locked oscillators are extensively utilized in spectroscopy, photochemistry, and laser physics. This study introduces a straightforward and precise method for measuring the temporal intensity profile of these pulses using a single-shot camera. The approach leverages the well-established and highly accurate technique for determining pulse chirp. Specifically, we measure the pulse's temporal intensity distribution by recording the radial energy density of the pulse when focused through a thin lens. This technique is straightforward, requires no adjustments, and achieves a measurement accuracy of approximately 1%. We demonstrate the method by characterizing the temporal intensity profile of a 10-fs pulse generated via a self-imaging interferogram. The findings indicate that this approach is effective for measuring pulses with durations exceeding 1 fs, provided the pulse energy exceeds 10 nJ. Furthermore, we show that this technique can identify and quantify the impact of satellite pulses. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of a single-shot camera for directly measuring the temporal intensity profile of Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillator pulses. Ultimately, we conclude that this method is well-suited for optimizing laser sources and diagnosing pulse shaping experiments. This study introduces a general analytical model to calculate the absorption profile within thin-film photovoltaic (TFPV) structures incorporating one-dimensional (1D) photonic crystals (PCs). The framework is applicable to any thin-film TFPV design, enabling the optimization of photonic crystal (PC) geometries to maximize light absorption across the entire solar spectrum. Consequently, the findings suggest that 1D PCs represent a more practical solution for achieving enhanced light absorption in thin-film TFPVs. The proposed modeling methodology is also transferable to other thin-film photonic devices. In summary, this research demonstrates that optimizing PC geometries enables 1D photonic structures to effectively trap light in thin silicon films, rendering them a viable alternative to 2D PCs. This approach yields explicit HDXs with bounded geometric parameters across arbitrary dimensions, featuring linear gauge sets, a diameter of logarithmic size, and polynomial degree. Additionally, these structures exhibit a length of linear size, which is optimal, alongside a length-width tradeoff that is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors. This outcome is achieved with an expansion factor of only poly(d), where d represents the dimension. Furthermore, this result is derived as a direct consequence of a broader finding: a technique for hypergraph sparsification that maintains expansion properties across all short sets. This method produces sparsifiers with a number of edges of O(m log n), a sparsification factor of O(log n), and a length-width tradeoff of at most O(d log n). Leveraging this sparsifier, we also construct explicit HDXs for graphs with arbitrary length-width tradeoffs, achieving a sparsification factor of O(d log n) and a number of edges of O(m log n). These outcomes are derived by combining our sparsifier with existing constructions of graphs possessing arbitrary length-width tradeoffs. Finally, we demonstrate that this sparsification technique is robust, enabling the preservation of a wide range of hypergraph properties for all short sets, including linear algebraic properties, cut-sparsification, and uniform edge distribution. This capability allows us to maintain the spectral properties of a given HDX while sparsifying it, a result that is crucial for applications in locally testable codes and property testing. In this context, our sparsification achieves a complexity of O(d log n) and requires only O(ε⁻²) queries. Notably, this result is the first to provide explicit construction and relies entirely on classical techniques, avoiding the use of random oracles. This distinct approach offers a significant advantage in locally testable code constructions, as it eliminates the need for random oracles, which are typically employed to establish explicit HDXs. By sparsifying existing explicit constructions, we obtain explicit locally testable codes with a testability factor of O(d log n) and a relative distance of O(ε²), utilizing a query complexity of O(ε⁻²). This improves upon the previous best-known testability factor of O(d²) and matches the efficiency of the best known explicit construction. Moreover, our explicit construction is the first to achieve a testability factor of O(d log n) without relying on random oracles.

In contrast to earlier models used for polarization-multiplexed 2D formats, this approach achieves an average deviation of less than 0.1 dB when compared against split-step Fourier simulations. Furthermore, the model's coefficients can be determined using a single set of measurements obtained via the Gaussian method. These characteristics make the model particularly valuable for optimizing transmission parameters in diverse 4D modulation schemes. Power optimization yields a significant performance improvement, reducing the required average launch power by 0.4 dB for a target BER of 10^-3. These results confirm that both power allocation and polarization rotation are effective tools for enhancing 4D transmission performance. Specifically, the terrain is represented as a collection of frictionally connected rigid bodies, while the robot is modeled as a rigid body interacting with the terrain via wheels. By integrating the equations of motion for both the robot and the terrain features, the system dynamics are formulated to include frictional contact forces. These simulations illustrate how the trajectories are influenced by various factors, including friction coefficients, frictional slip, and the resulting frictional dissipation. The results indicate that the method is particularly effective in modeling the stick-slip behavior of robots on rough terrain. This research serves as a foundation for future investigations into more complex scenarios, such as those involving flexible bodies, unmodeled dynamics, and stick-slip phenomena. In the classical limit, the quantum Hamiltonian for this system is given by $H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac{k}{2}x\cdot Kx$, where $K$ represents a circulant matrix. The matrix $K$ possesses eigenvalues $0$ with multiplicity $2$ and $2$ with multiplicity $N-2$. Consequently, the Hamiltonian $H$ exhibits $N-2$ distinct pairs of eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues of $0$ and the remaining $2$ eigenvectors corresponding to non-zero eigenvalues. The two eigenvectors associated with eigenvalue $0$ represent the eigenspace of the symmetry group $Z_N$. The first eigenvector corresponds to the totally symmetric state, while the second corresponds to the totally antisymmetric state. The other $2(N-2)$ eigenvectors are organized into $N-2$ pairs, where each pair consists of eigenvectors with eigenvalues $E_j$ and $E_j^*$. These pairs are related by complex conjugation. The $2(N-2)$ eigenvectors with non-zero eigenvalues are arranged into $N-2$ pairs, where each pair comprises eigenvectors with eigenvalues $E_j$ and $E_j^*$. The eigenvectors with eigenvalues $E_j$ and $E_j^*$ are defined by the formula $x_{n,j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{l=1}^N\omega^{(j-1)(n-1)}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi l}{N}\right)\sin\left(\frac{2\pi (l-1)}{N}\right)$, where $\omega=e^{i\frac{2\pi}{N}}$. The eigenvalues are given by $E_j=k\left(1+\frac{1}{\omega^{j-1}}\right)$ for $j=2,\dots,N$. The spectrum of the classical ring is characterized by $2(N-2)$ degenerate frequencies, where each frequency $\omega_j=\sqrt{E_j}$ has a degenerate partner $\omega_j^*=\sqrt{E_j^*}$. Universality (LFU) ratio, $R_\Sigma$, for $B\to X_{\rm had}$ decays, derived from the sum of ratios across all kinematically accessible hadronic final states. This observable is evaluated within the $SU(3)_C$ flavour symmetry limit and examined through various $B$ meson decays, including those involving vector mesons, scalar mesons, and pions. Leveraging the complete set of $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s)$ QCD corrections and incorporating corrections for breaking flavour symmetries, we predict $R_\Sigma = 0.998\pm 0.010$. These findings are compared against recent experimental measurements from the LHCb and Belle collaborations. Additionally, we explore potential new physics contributions to $R_\Sigma$ arising from both scalar and vector operators. Finally, we assess the utility of $R_\Sigma$ as a probe for new physics in the context of current experimental data. Our analysis demonstrates that $R_\Sigma$ offers a clean test of the Standard Model, with an expected total uncertainty of approximately 1%, making it a promising tool for investigating new physics effects. Furthermore, we note that recent data from LHCb and Belle show a mild preference for a value of $R_\Sigma$ differing from the SM prediction, which could signal the presence of new physics. However, these results remain inconsistent with the current experimental status of $R_{K^\pm}$ and $R_{K^*}$, suggesting that any new physics scenario must involve a complex interplay of hadronic effects. Future measurements of $R_\Sigma$ are anticipated to provide a valuable new avenue for searching for physics beyond the Standard Model. 20% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) exhibit signs of pulmonary vascular disease, a condition that may worsen IPF prognosis. However, the specific characteristics of this vascular abnormality in IPF remain poorly understood. **Objectives:** To characterize pulmonary vascular involvement in IPF and assess its impact on IPF outcomes. **Methods:** We conducted a retrospective analysis of 100 IPF patients who underwent high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) at a single center. Vascular abnormalities were categorized into three types: (1) irregularity, (2) narrowing, and (3) occlusion. **Results:** Irregular vessels were observed in 40% of IPF cases, while narrowing and occlusion occurred in 10% and 10% of cases, respectively. Irregular vessels were more prevalent in IPF patients with greater lung volume loss, lower diffusing capacity, and higher 6-minute walk distance. Notably, irregular vessels were associated with a significantly higher mortality risk (hazard ratio: 2.4; 95% confidence interval: 1.2–4.9). **Conclusions:** Irregular pulmonary vessels are a common finding in IPF and are linked to increased mortality. These findings suggest that irregular vessels represent a distinct vascular pathology that may influence IPF prognosis. **Keywords:** Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; Pulmonary vascular abnormalities; Irregular vessels; Prognosis.

This study investigates how surface termination affects SOC in the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ family. By employing first-principles calculations, we analyze the SOC bands for various surface terminations within the (211) superlattice. Our findings reveal that SOC bands are highly sensitive to surface termination, with the Bi-terminated surface exhibiting the strongest SOC and Se-terminated surfaces showing the weakest. These results are explained by the distinct symmetries of the Bi and Se surface states. Furthermore, we observe that SOC bands with lower symmetry demonstrate a greater dependence on the number of quantum wells in the superlattice. Finally, we demonstrate that SOC bands can be effectively tuned by adjusting the thickness of the quantum well. These insights are anticipated to aid in the design of novel topological insulator devices.

We demonstrate that the model's Hamiltonian is governed by a non-trivial fixed point, which we identify as a new type of supersymmetric fixed point. are extensively utilized for developing quantum devices, including superconducting qubits and topological qubits. However, determining the precise location of the induced superconducting gap within the semiconductor channel remains difficult. This study examines quantum-coherent transport in a quantum point contact fabricated from a 2D electron gas in Si/MoSi using a voltage-biased four-terminal configuration. We observe that the conductance exhibits a finite offset at zero bias temperature, which we attribute to a spatially non-uniform superconducting proximity effect. By analyzing how this offset varies with temperature and frequency, we extract the local superconducting gap size and its temperature dependence specifically at the measurement point. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the offset scales with temperature according to a Fermi-Dirac distribution, consistent with tunneling through a local superconducting gap. This methodology provides a reliable means to quantify the local superconducting gap in quantum devices, facilitating the design of devices with optimized performance. Additionally, our results indicate that the offset is governed by the semiconductor's local density of states near the Fermi level, suggesting that the gap can be enhanced by moving away from the metallic phase. This insight is particularly valuable for topological quantum devices, where the semiconductor is typically biased to avoid the metallic phase to promote the emergence of topological edge states. Finally, we show that the conductance spectrum can be accurately described by a non-equilibrium Green's function model incorporating a non-zero chemical potential offset. This modeling approach offers a straightforward method to characterize transport in these devices and to extract the local superconducting gap size and its temperature dependence. These findings are particularly relevant for topological quantum devices, where a non-zero offset is essential for the non-equilibrium generation of topological Majorana modes. In summary, this work provides a comprehensive characterization of quantum transport through a 1D electron channel with a non-uniformly induced superconducting gap, offering a pathway to quantify gap properties at specific locations. This capability is crucial for designing quantum devices and for investigating the spatial distribution of the induced superconducting gap. This study investigates the chemical and physical consequences of these stellar X-rays on disk chemistry, focusing on the formation of complex organic molecules (COMs) and their precursors. In this approach, radiation friction is derived from the quantum Langevin equation, which comprises two components: the primary radiation pressure term and a memory kernel representing vacuum fluctuations. This memory term is frequently overlooked, yet it becomes significant in strong fields. We demonstrate that when properly accounted for, this memory term cancels the nonphysical negative kinetic energy losses that the primary radiation pressure term alone can produce. Furthermore, we show that the inclusion of the memory term ensures the strong-field expansion yields a unique solution. Finally, we apply this methodology to examine radiation friction during linear motion. In this context, the memory term can be explicitly calculated and is essential for correctly describing the self-force. We find that, unlike in the linear case, the memory term vanishes during circular motion in strong fields. This absence explains why the circular motion solution is unique and why radiation friction remains independent of the memory term. These findings are corroborated by numerical simulations of the Langevin equation. Our study establishes a foundation for a rigorous and unambiguous calculation of radiation friction in strong fields. Additionally, the developed formalism may prove valuable for modeling stochastic processes of charged particles in strong fields, such as those encountered in accelerators. A critical challenge in network science is identifying the specific mechanisms that generate these networks. While statistical models have been developed to explain various network types, they often lack a clear description of the underlying generative process. This paper introduces a new class of network models termed "network games." These games are defined by a network of potential interactions between players, where each player selects a strategy that determines their active interactions. The resulting network structure is dictated by the players' strategies and the payoff they generate. We demonstrate that when players engage in a network game involving a finite number of players and strategies, the corresponding payoff matrix must possess a specific property: it must be totally balanced. Furthermore, we establish that if this condition is met, the set of possible network structures and their associated payoffs is both closed and convex. Finally, we provide a method for solving such MMDPs. The paper concludes by outlining open questions and potential applications of network games. This study examines the validity of the no-slip condition for liquid flow through a slit formed by two parallel plates, where the liquid-vapor interface is pinned to the plate surfaces. We demonstrate that, within the framework of continuum mechanics, the no-slip condition holds true under this specific geometry. This finding contrasts with noether's theorem, which indicates that no-slip is not generally valid at liquid-solid interfaces. The implications of our result for micro- and nanofluidic applications are discussed. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the validity of no-slip depends on the specific form of the intermolecular potential used to describe liquid-solid interactions. This insight may assist in developing more accurate continuum models that incorporate liquid-solid interactions. Finally, our results suggest that the validity of no-slip at liquid-solid interfaces warrants further investigation. We have made our software available for public use. kidney disease (CKD) has been largely overlooked. This study aimed to identify critical periods during early life that influence CKD risk in adulthood. Utilizing data from 1,000 participants in the Cardiovascular Risk in Young Adults study, we applied Cox proportional hazards models to track time-to-event trajectories for CKD. We assessed associations between childhood risk factors and adult CKD, incorporating mediation analysis to evaluate how adult risk factors explained these links.

The analysis revealed that higher systolic blood pressure (SBP) and fasting glucose levels in adulthood were strongly linked to increased CKD risk, whereas higher high-density lipoprotein cholesterol was protective. Crucially, these adult risk factors mediated a substantial portion of the risk associated with childhood SBP and fasting glucose. Specifically, adult SBP mediated 30% and adult fasting glucose mediated 28% of the risk from childhood SBP; meanwhile, adult SBP and fasting glucose jointly mediated 44% of the risk stemming from childhood fasting glucose.

In conclusion, the relationship between childhood metabolic and hemodynamic risk factors and adult CKD is heavily mediated by their adult counterparts. These findings underscore the need for early-life prevention strategies targeting cardiovascular risk factors to reduce future CKD incidence. Furthermore, adult cardiovascular risk factors should be considered as potential contributors to CKD progression. This study presents the first observational evidence of a warm-climate state characterized by a weak Hadley circulation. Utilizing a comprehensive global reanalysis dataset, we identified a distinct shift in the mean latitude of the Hadley cell boundary from its typical ~25° to an unusually low ~15° during the exceptionally warm summers of 2003 and 2010. This northward contraction of the Hadley cell was driven by a reduction in the equator-to-pole temperature gradient caused by the anomalous warmth. Consequently, future climate models must accurately simulate the dynamical response of the Hadley circulation to elevated global temperatures. We introduce a method to represent such non-terminating functions using two components: (1) a terminating program paired with annotations, and (2) a termination argument. This paper primarily addresses the verification of these annotated programs. We propose a novel technique for annotating recursive functions with termination hypotheses to facilitate the automatic derivation of non-terminating behavior. These solitons sustain a zero mode corresponding to an internal degree of freedom, which manifests as an extra $U(1)$ symmetry in the two-field system. This internal symmetry remains intact due to the specific form of the mass-like coupling. By employing a dual field representation, we establish that the zero mode symmetry corresponds to the self-duality of the field equations, thereby yielding an upper bound on the soliton energy. Our findings indicate that this system exhibits a sequence of phases: a spin-polarized ferromagnetic state at low electron densities, a spin-polarized semiconducting state at intermediate densities, and an antiferromagnetically ordered state at high densities. Its origin remains a subject of debate, with two primary hypotheses: either it is a single supernova remnant or a complex structure formed by the interaction of multiple supernova remnants. This study aims to constrain the age of Sgr A East to differentiate between these scenarios. We employed a multi-wavelength approach, analyzing X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the XMM-Newton satellite, alongside radio observations from the Very Large Array and the Australia Telescope Compact Array. By utilizing a novel method that accounts for the age-dependent morphology of supernova remnants, we determined that Sgr A East is approximately 100,000 years old. This age aligns with the timeline of the Sun's formation, suggesting a potential link between the two. Furthermore, the derived age indicates that Sgr A East is unlikely to be a single supernova remnant. Our findings are consistent with the multi-wavelength data available in the literature and support the hypothesis that Sgr A East comprises multiple supernova remnants. Additionally, we identified a new radio lobe within the remnant, which we estimate to be roughly 100,000 years old. This age matches that of the supernova responsible for the lobe, implying that the lobe is also a remnant of a separate supernova. Finally, we calculated the distance to the center of the remnant as 8.1 kpc, a value that agrees with other established distance estimates. These results are also consistent with the hypothesis that Sgr A East is formed by multiple supernova remnants. Specifically, given an n-vertex convex geometric graph G with maximum degree d and a family F of k-dimensional convex bodies, the goal is to find a weight-maximizing independent set, where each vertex v is associated with a body f(v) in F, and two vertices are adjacent if their corresponding bodies intersect. We demonstrate that for any fixed dimension d and any ε > 0, kVIS can be solved in O(n^(d-1+ε)) time. Furthermore, we prove a similar EPTAS for the k-Dimensional Maximum Weight Clique (k-MWC) problem on the same graph type, yielding an O(n^(d-1+ε)) time solution. Additionally, we present a constant-factor approximation algorithm for both k-VIS and k-MWC on convex geometric graphs with bounded vertex degree that runs in O(n log n) time. Finally, we introduce a constant-factor approximation algorithm for the Minimum Weight k-Center Problem (MWkCP) on point sets in R^d, solvable in O(n^(d-1+ε)) time. These findings significantly extend prior results from planar graphs and unit disk graphs to the broader category of convex geometric graphs with bounded degree. All algorithms discussed are deterministic. The core technique involves a new approach to constant-factor approximating the Independent Set problem on graphs of bounded treewidth, which may be of independent interest. This method relies on a novel concept of "separable" vertex sets within trees of bounded treewidth, which we define and provide characterizations for. t\bar{t}$) production at the LHC is typically calculated using next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) QCD predictions, which are validated against experimental data. This study presents a comprehensive comparison of theoretical predictions against ALPS Collaboration data from the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The measurement was conducted at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, utilizing a data set corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis employed a data-driven technique to determine the acceptance and efficiency of the selected events. The resulting cross-section, along with differential measurements, are presented as a function of the invariant mass of the $t\bar{t}$ system. Theoretical predictions for the inclusive and differential cross-sections were generated using various methods for calculating higher-order QCD corrections. However, determining how geometric chirality influences the formation of matter remains an unresolved challenge across various disciplines, including the self-assembly of colloidal particles, liquid crystalline phases, and the mechanics of thin shells. This study introduces a straightforward yet robust theoretical framework for analyzing how geometric chirality drives matter formation. The framework utilizes a one-dimensional model featuring both extensional and bending stiffness, solved through an energy minimization approach. It demonstrates that even minor deviations from symmetry can trigger significant effects from geometric chirality, resulting in diverse phenomena such as non-planar configurations, multiple equilibrium states, and symmetry-breaking transitions. The model's applicability is confirmed by its ability to accurately describe the shape and stability of twisted rods, deformed shells, and corrugated ribbons. These findings suggest that one-dimensional models can effectively capture the essential physics of how geometric chirality governs the formation of chiral matter. Furthermore, this approach offers a foundation for designing synthetic structures with tailored shapes and functionalities, such as self-actuated shells and stretchable electronics. The availability of the associated code and data supports these conclusions. In summary, we present a simple energy model for 1D objects that effectively explains how geometric chirality dictates the formation of matter. This methodology is broadly applicable to a wide range of systems, including extensional and bending-stiff rods, shells, and sheets. We show that simple chirality can induce complex behaviors, even in systems possessing additional material chirality. Our findings indicate that understanding how geometric chirality forms matter is fundamentally a one-dimensional problem, a conclusion validated by comparisons with existing literature. We anticipate that the insights gained from this simplified model will facilitate the design of diverse materials capable of shape-shifting in response to external stimuli. This process is characterized by the spontaneous emergence of a rough growth front, which can be described by a roughness exponent of approximately 0.33. This study provides a comprehensive quantitative analysis of the dynamics of such rough fronts, utilizing high-resolution imaging and advanced statistical methods. The objective is to minimize the space complexity and query time of the resulting structure.

Our primary contribution is a new approach to building linear-time linear-space exact near neighbor structures, which we then adapt to create efficient approximate versions. This method relies on a novel technique for decomposing point sets into well-separated clusters, where the distance between clusters is nearly proportional to the distance between any two points within the same cluster. This decomposition is achieved through a new algorithm for the $k$-means clustering problem.

As a result, we present the first exact near neighbor structure operating in linear space with polylogarithmic query time, achieving a success probability of $1-\delta$ within $O(\frac{\log n}{\delta})$ queries. Furthermore, we provide a highly efficient approximate structure with success probability $1-\delta$ and $O(\frac{\log n}{\delta^2})$ query time. Both structures achieve linear space complexity, improving upon the previously best-known linear-space exact structure that required $O(\log n / \delta)$ query time. Additionally, our linear-space approximate structure surpasses the performance of the prior state-of-the-art exact near neighbor structure.

Our structures are derived by adapting a recent exact near neighbor structure by Gupta et al. (2019), which utilized the recursive tree construction method of Clarkson and Shi (2010). We demonstrate that Gupta et al.'s structure can be modified to achieve linear space complexity by employing a new, linear-space version of the Clarkson-Shi method. This adaptation relies on our novel clustering-based decomposition of point sets into well-separated clusters, which is the core contribution of this paper.

Finally, we show that the linear-space exact near neighbor structure can be converted into an efficient approximate structure by applying a straightforward technique introduced by Neiman and Wulff-Nilsen (2020). This process involves repeatedly querying the exact structure until a sufficiently accurate near neighbor is found. This reduction yields the aforementioned efficient approximate structure and represents the first application of this technique to the near neighbor problem. Our approach improves upon the prior

This paper introduces a novel wirelessly-enabled cloud computing framework designed to mitigate the high energy consumption associated with wireless access. By utilizing multiple remote radio heads (RRHs) to provide coverage, the system ensures that every user can offload tasks to the cloud. We propose a two-stage optimization strategy aimed at minimizing total energy usage. In the first stage, the optimal number of active RRHs is determined. In the second stage, we jointly optimize the offloading rates and the power consumption of these active RRHs. This joint optimization is modeled as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem, which is subsequently decomposed into two distinct subproblems. Since the offloading rate subproblem is non-convex, we introduce a new algorithm to derive the optimal solution. For the power consumption subproblem, we apply the first-order Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions to achieve optimality. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed approach effectively reduces energy consumption. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of various offloading rate allocation schemes and compare them against a benchmark scenario. Our findings indicate that the proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in energy usage while satisfying all offloading rate requirements. Additionally, the results show that the offloading rate allocation scheme yields the most significant energy savings. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithm through comprehensive simulation studies. These studies reveal that the number of required RRHs is directly proportional to the offloading rate, and that a uniform power allocation strategy is more energy-efficient than a proportional one. Overall, the proposed algorithm is highly effective in reducing energy consumption. The simulation outcomes confirm that the system can successfully meet the offloading rate requirements of all users. This research offers valuable insights for the design and deployment of wirelessly-enabled cloud computing systems. Our proposed algorithm is particularly well-suited for applications where energy consumption is a critical constraint. Furthermore, the methodology can be extended to other wireless systems, such as wireless sensor networks and vehicular networks, to achieve similar energy efficiency benefits. We introduce a novel adversarial attack termed \textit{Contextual Arm Permutation Attack} (COPA), which forces users to swap action rewards without revealing the reasons for their preferences. COPA aims to degrade the learner by minimizing its regret. We demonstrate that a polynomial number of queries are sufficient for the attacker to completely destroy the learner's context information, resulting in regret equivalent to that of a vacuum learner. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on queries required to achieve any regret improvement over the vacuum learner. Our findings indicate that while the learner can recover from this attack with exponentially many queries, the attacker can still achieve a significant reduction in learner regret with a sub-polynomial number of queries. These results are derived for both adversarial and adversarial-bandit variants of COPA. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our theory aligns with experimental outcomes, revealing that COPA is highly effective at reducing both the learner's regret and the number of queries needed to recover from the attack. These insights advance our understanding of adversarial impacts within CB frameworks. -ray pulse at room temperature generates a significant impulsive excitation of the core-hole state, which triggers the coherent motion of valence electrons. This phenomenon is demonstrated through time-resolved x-ray absorption spectroscopy of the 3d transition metal oxide LaMnO$_3$, utilizing self-amplified spontaneous emission (SASE) free-electron laser pulses. The observed coherent x-ray excitation is confirmed by measuring the x-ray transient's duration with sub-attosecond precision using attosecond pulses from the SASE pulses. The excitation's time evolution is interpreted as the coherent oscillation of the 3d $e_g$ orbital, driven by the x-ray pulse and mediated by the 3d-4p energy gap. This study marks the first observation of a coherent orbital state in a correlated oxide and the inaugural measurement of an orbital lifetime in the attosecond range. These findings establish a foundation for developing coherent light sources and x-ray pulse shaping for quantum control of electronic states. Furthermore, the experiment demonstrates that the electronic excitation time of an x-ray excited orbital can be precisely controlled by manipulating the x-ray pulse spectrum. This capability is expected to enable the study of coherent light-matter interactions in quantum materials. Additionally, the study presents a novel method for measuring the x-ray transient time of a core excitation using valence orbital resonances in the near-edge region, offering a promising alternative to pump-probe experiments that rely on pump pulses at the same photon energy. Finally, the research confirms the potential of free-electron laser pulses for x-ray quantum control. The core excitation time of approximately 100 as is comparable to the x-ray pulse duration, indicating that the core excitation process itself is non-impulsive. This non-impulsive nature may be crucial for the coherent orbital excitation and could facilitate the realization of a coherent light microscope. This paper introduces a novel approach to reduce the memory footprint of DNN-based ASR models by leveraging the inherent redundancy within them. We propose a new algorithm called Tensor Rank Minimization (TRM) that approximates the DNN's core tensor using a low-rank decomposition. TRM offers specific advantages over existing low-rank approximation techniques, such as Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), particularly for models with multiple input dimensions. Furthermore, the proposed method supports the compression of both trained and fine-tuned models. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields a superior cost-to-performance ratio compared to prior techniques. Specifically, a compression rate of 5.5x was achieved with minimal degradation in Word Error Rate (WER) relative to the baseline. Additionally, the proposed method effectively mitigates the substantial memory requirements associated with the fine-tuning process. Additionally, we establish a continuity criterion for singular measures on manifolds and the plane, offering a streamlined proof of the planar result by Figalli, Juutinen, and Sverak. Our methodology relies on comparing the lengths of geodesics within the space of measures. This approach is fundamentally rooted in the observation that the second variation of length along geodesics in a positively curved space is upper-bounded by the second variation computed via the formal Riemannian metric, a principle originally due to Fenchel and Eisenhart. This insight enables us to derive a straightforward sufficient condition for Alexandrov's metric continuity that is notably less restrictive than previously known criteria. Specifically, we demonstrate that the MTW condition ensures sufficient "curvature" to maintain metric comparison, a result that is striking given the abstract nature of this condition and its reliance on a non-Euclidean, partially ordered metric tensor. Furthermore, we prove that for regular measures on two-dimensional manifolds, metric comparison holds even without requiring the second variation to remain non-negative. The proofs are notably concise, utilizing the properties of Hilbert–Segal–Ward's energy and the regularity of the optimal map. In the singular setting, we extend the concept of a Kantorovich dual potential to apply to singular measures, thereby deriving a comparison criterion for the length of geodesics in the space of measures. This criterion is sufficiently robust to guarantee metric comparison for specific classes of singular measures. The findings are notably practical, as they allow us to verify the necessary regularity of these measures to ensure the continuity of the optimal transport map. In summary, we establish that the length of geodesics in the space of measures is continuous under the Hausdorff topology for a broad class of measures, encompassing both regular and singular cases. This result is achieved by establishing a link to the "curvature" of the space via a generalized MTW condition and leveraging the regularity of the measures. The study of this new comparison and its implications for the continuity of the optimal transport map will be the focus of a subsequent paper. If PBHs exist, they would emit Hawking radiation, with smaller masses corresponding to higher emission rates and temperatures. This radiative output can be detected through various channels, including gamma rays, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. This review examines the theoretical and observational evidence regarding PBHs as dark matter, with a specific focus on gravitational wave signatures. The repulsion is derived from the dimerization of monomers with hard-sphere cores, while the attraction arises from the self-assembly of tetramers formed by linking dimers. Our results indicate that the competition between these attractive and repulsive interactions drives the system's phase behavior. Specifically, as attractive interactions are gradually introduced, the repulsion weakly stabilizes the bulk liquid phase, triggering a gas-liquid critical point. Further increasing attraction causes this critical point to shift toward higher densities. Eventually, the bulk gas becomes unstable, giving rise to a bicontinuous gas-bulk liquid coexistence region. Subsequently, the bulk liquid phase destabilizes, leading to the emergence of a bicontinuous gas-liquid-bulk solid (tetramer crystal) phase diagram. Finally, we demonstrate that the bulk liquid- tetramer crystal transition is first-order, with a spinodal decomposition scenario occurring at the triple point. These findings offer a theoretical basis for understanding the phase behavior of complex biological systems, such as cytoskeletal networks. In this context, dimers represent the basic units of the system, while tetramers correspond to the structures formed by dimer assembly. Furthermore, our study reveals that the competition between repulsive and attractive interactions can induce a bicontinuous gas-liquid-solid phase diagram, a phenomenon observed in various cytoskeletal systems. This competition is responsible for the unusual phase behavior of these biological structures. Additionally, we show that the proposed model can be experimentally realized using DNA-origami nanostructures. These outcomes offer a theoretical framework for comprehending the phase behavior of cytoskeletal systems. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this model in designing cytoskeletal-like materials. We demonstrate that for sufficiently large $n$, the critical distance from any codeword is approximately $1 - e^{-k} + o(1)$. This study examines power spectrum effects arising from two specific two-scale inflation models: one governed by a light inflaton and another by a dark energy field. We analyze how these two distinct mechanisms influence the power spectrum and assess the resulting constraints on the model parameter space. Furthermore, we explore the potential for these models to be identified through the combined analysis of cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies and large-scale structure (LSS). Specifically, we demonstrate that the best-fit parameters for both two-scale models can be simultaneously constrained using current CMB and LSS data. Additionally, we show that the dark energy model can be distinguished from the light inflaton model by combining CMB and LSS observations. Finally, we illustrate that combining current CMB and LSS data enhances our ability to detect two-scale inflation models and to constrain their parameter space. Deep learning has become the standard for medical image analysis, yet these models often function as opaque "black boxes," making it difficult to understand the visual features driving their decisions. This lack of transparency is especially problematic in the high-stakes context of clinical decision-making. This paper presents a new approach to improve the interpretability of the popular ResNet architecture. Our method utilizes a multi-scale attention mechanism, enabling the model to concentrate on pertinent regions of the visual input. We evaluated this technique on the Pathology Triage dataset, where it outperforms current state-of-the-art results with a sensitivity of 84.3% at 90% specificity. Furthermore, the attention maps produced by our model highlight the regions of interest. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves the interpretability of deep learning models. The code can be found at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/attentional-resnet.

Specifically, we demonstrate that the exponential decay of solutions in the primal problem is directly related to the rapid growth of solutions in the dual problem. This finding allows us to re-examine several established results regarding the exponential stability of the Cauchy problem for parabolic, hyperbolic, and thermoelastic systems. Furthermore, we apply this approach to investigate the exponential stability of a system modeling heat conduction with memory and size effects, which is formulated as a third-order system of partial differential equations. In this application, we derive a precise relationship between the solutions of the primal problem and the solutions of the dual problem. Finally, we illustrate how the stability results are influenced by the spectral properties of the generator of the contraction semi-group. To achieve these results, we employ tools from operator theory, functional analysis, spectral theory, and duality. Notably, we utilize the concept of the resolvent growth index to characterize the exponential decay rate of contraction semi-groups. Additionally, we establish a link between the resolvent growth index and the solutions of dual problems to derive sufficient conditions for well-posedness that ensure the exponential stability of the Cauchy problem. This allows us to determine sufficient conditions for the exponential stability of the Cauchy problem for various well-known systems. For practical applications, we also provide a characterization of the resolvent growth index based on the behavior of resolvent norms. This final result is significant because it enables the investigation of the exponential stability of the Cauchy problem for contraction semi-groups without requiring the explicit computation of resolvent norms. By applying this characterization, we demonstrate that the solutions of dual problems exhibit rapid growth when the Cauchy problem lacks exponential stability. This finding is particularly valuable for studying the exponential stability of third-order systems, where solutions typically grow rapidly. In contrast to existing literature, which often relies on the logarithmic convexity principle, our results offer a novel and alternative method for investigating the exponential stability of the Cauchy problem. Our findings are supported by rigorous theoretical proofs and detailed examples. Through this framework, we can effectively analyze the stability properties of contraction semi-groups and their duals, providing a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between primal and dual systems. This understanding is crucial for advancing the theoretical foundations of various physical systems and engineering applications. Overall, this research contributes to the broader field of mathematical physics and engineering by offering new insights into the stability properties of contraction semi-groups and their duals, with potential applications in fluid dynamics, elasticity theory, and other areas

### 1. Introduction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into various domains, including healthcare, finance, and transportation. However, the widespread adoption of AI systems necessitates their reliability and robustness. Despite this, developing reliable AI systems remains a significant challenge due to the complexity of their architectures and the vast volume of data they process. These factors make it difficult to predict model behavior and determine the root causes of failures. This paper addresses the general problem of diagnosing AI models to identify the source of errors. We propose a framework that localizes faults by analyzing a fault-agnostic representation of the AI model, referred to as a "sketch." This sketch is derived from a decision tree model that abstracts the input-output behavior of the original AI model. We demonstrate that this sketch can be used to pinpoint the root cause of failures within the AI system. Our approach is evaluated on multiple datasets across different domains, including image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. The results show that our method effectively identifies the root cause of failures in AI applications. Additionally, we prove that our decision tree-based sketching approach

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of the expected number of k-jets in two specific models of k-dimensional excursion surfaces defined over d-dimensional domains. The first model involves the planar (d=2) k-jets of a two-dimensional Ising (NEE) excursion surface, while the second addresses the k-jets of a one-dimensional Ising (NEE) excursion surface in any d>2 dimensions. We establish that for the first model, the asymptotic value of the mean number of k-jets is exponential in the domain's area, whereas for the second model, it is quadratic in the domain's perimeter. Additionally, we provide an exact formula for the case where k=d=3 for the first model and d=3 for the second model. These findings highlight that the asymptotic behavior of k-jet counts is contingent upon both the dimensionality of the excursion surface and that of the excising domain. Our results further support a broader conjecture regarding the universal behavior of k-jet counts across excursion surfaces within the mean-field universality class. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these results to the theory of random tilings and the analysis of dislocation structures in crystalline solids. The paper also includes an analysis of the universal behavior of k-jet counts in the more complex scenario where the excursion surface and excising domain reside in different universality classes. In this context, we demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior of the mean number of k-jets remains the same as in the mean-field case whenever the dimension of the excising domain is strictly greater than 2. While dynamic networks have been extensively studied in recent years, few efforts have focused on modeling the simultaneous changes in directionality and weight distribution. This paper introduces a directed, weighted network model featuring dynamic directionality and decay mechanisms for both edge weights and edge flows. These decay processes are balanced by attachment mechanisms that create new edges to ensure the network grows and remains connected. The decay dynamics lead to a power-law distribution of edge weights, whereas directionality decays disproportionately affect short edges, resulting in a significant increase in the proportion of long directed edges. Additionally, we propose a method to estimate the decay and attachment parameters using network snapshots, enabling the backtracking of network evolution from historical data. We validate this estimation method using synthetic data and apply it to two real-world networks: the CiteSeerx citation network and the Enron email network. The accuracy of the backtracking results is evaluated by comparing key network metrics between the original dynamic evolution and the reconstructed one. The study demonstrates that the proposed model can effectively reconstruct the evolution of large-scale networks and serves as a foundation for future research on dynamic directed and weighted networks. Furthermore, the estimation approach is shown to be broadly applicable to various networks, regardless of their specific structures. Finally, we provide an open-source Python package containing the model implementation and backtracking tools to facilitate further research. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengy021/DW-DynNet.

**1. Introduction**  
Complex networks, characterized by their dynamic and heterogeneous nature, are widely observed across diverse fields including the social sciences, physics, and biology. These networks are typically represented as graphs where nodes represent entities and edges represent their interactions. However, traditional graph models often fail to capture the full dynamics of real-world systems. For instance, graphs are generally unweighted, whereas many real-world interactions possess varying strengths. Furthermore, while graphs can represent directionality, they often overlook the dynamic nature of these directed edges.

To address these limitations, dynamic and weighted networks have emerged as more realistic models. In these frameworks, edge weights evolve over time, leading to phenomena such as preferential attachment where nodes with higher degrees attract more edges. These models have been applied to diverse systems, including social networks, where they reveal that interactions between highly connected individuals are more likely to persist

Our approach relies on the analytic characteristics of the Green's function within the complex frequency domain. Specifically, we demonstrate that the presence of superconductivity is indicated by the emergence of a pole in the superconducting frequency component of the Green's function, a feature absent in gapless systems. We apply this framework to investigate superconductivity in the Kekulé-distorted graphene honeycomb lattice. Our findings indicate that while the pristine system remains gapless, the distorted configuration exhibits superconductivity at zero temperature, despite the absence of Fermi surface nesting. Additionally, we examine the impact of chemical potential variations on the LDOS and conclude that the Kekulé distortion genuinely induces a superconducting state in graphene. These insights are applicable to other two-dimensional materials featuring hexagonal symmetry. Finally, we outline the necessary modifications to extend this form of spectroscopy to experimental settings. These changes involve substituting the frequency variable $\omega$ with the real part of the complex energy in both the LDOS and the frequency-dependent components of the Green's function. We contend that this adjustment does not compromise the validity of the proposed formalism. Furthermore, we note that the resulting gapless signature in the LDOS is more pronounced than when utilizing the full complex variable $\omega$. This enhanced gapless signature could facilitate the observation of superconductivity in graphene through experiments measuring the frequency-dependent real part of the Green's function. Such measurements are feasible via tunneling spectroscopy using a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) equipped with a Josephson junction tip. Finally, we emphasize that the proposed formalism is not restricted to the specific model under study but is also applicable to gapless systems possessing a finite density of states at the chemical potential. We anticipate that this framework will enable the detection of superconductivity in novel materials, including topological insulators and Dirac/Weyl semimetals. Sun's rotation influences the development of magnetic fields and plasma structures within the corona. By analyzing the evolution of magnetic fields in a coronal loop model, we demonstrate that field rotation generates shear, thereby amplifying magnetic energy. We show that the coronal loop system is unstable under the combined effects of shear and gravity, leading to the formation of helical structures. Additionally, the initial twist of the magnetic field triggers an instability driven by the magnetic mirror effect. Our findings indicate that the magnetic field undergoes a transition from a simple helical configuration to a complex one featuring both helicity and tortuosity. These outcomes are significant for explaining the origins of solar coronal loops, the mechanism behind the emergence of magnetic bipoles, and the source of helicity observed in the corona. This study was conducted using the MHD code PLUTO. Our results suggest that the magnetic field in the corona possesses a more intricate structure than previously believed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnetic field in a coronal loop is not static but evolves over time. These insights may also assist in elucidating the magnetic field structure in the solar atmosphere. Finally, our results could contribute to understanding the mechanisms behind the formation of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and solar flares. This study examines the 1,2-addition of OH radicals to ethylene, a reaction critical for atmospheric chemistry and combustion modeling. By comparing high-level quantum chemical calculations with various dynamic approaches, we determined that the most accurate reaction rate is obtained using the MRCI+CASPT2 method for potential energy surfaces and the Semiclassical Trajectory (SCT) method for dynamics. This approach yields a rate constant of $k_{\text{SCT}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ at 298 K. Our findings indicate that the SCT method surpasses other techniques, including Quasi-classical Trajectories (QCT), Tunneling (TST), and Multi-Configuration Time-Dependent Hartree (MCTDH) calculations, which predict rates of $0.1 \times 10^{-10}$, $0.2 \times 10^{-10}$, and $0.3 \times 1$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$, respectively. We attribute the enhanced SCT performance to its inclusion of tunneling corrections and the accurate description of the post-transition complex. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reaction proceeds via a tunneling mechanism even at room temperature. Ultimately, this work underscores the necessity of combining precise quantum chemical surfaces with rigorous semi-classical dynamics to achieve accurate chemical rate constants. The proposed framework can be applied to similar reactions, such as OH addition to propene, to predict both major and minor product branching ratios. **1. Introduction**  
Text transformations are fundamental to numerous natural language processing tasks, including data augmentation, transfer learning, and bias mitigation. However, current approaches to defining these transformations predominantly rely on hand-crafted rules. For instance, common transformations like random token dropping, back translation, and synonym replacement are manually constructed. While effective, this hand-crafted nature restricts the generalizability of these transformations. To address this limitation, we propose a method for automatically generating text transformations. Specifically, we formulate transformation generation as an optimization task, where the objective function is tailored to a downstream application. We employ a recurrent neural network (RNN) to represent transformations and apply the Generalized Adversarial Transformation (GAT) technique to optimize the transformations based on our objective function. We validate the utility of these learned transformations across three applications: synthetic data generation, pseudo-labeling, and adversarial training. Our results indicate that synthetic data generated using optimized transformations outperforms those generated via standard transformations across multiple NLP tasks. Additionally, pseudo-labeling utilizing optimized transformations achieves superior results compared to those using pre-defined transformations. Finally, we observe that optimized transformations yield better performance in adversarial training scenarios than fixed transformations.

Additionally, adversarial training involves training models on transformed data to enhance robustness against adversarial attacks. $r$-uniform hypergraph $\mathcal{H}$, denoted $T(r, \mathcal{H})$, is defined as the maximum number of edges in an $\mathcal{H}$-free $r$-uniform hypergraph. This paper establishes a lower bound for $T(r, K^r_{r+1})$ that surpasses the longstanding Erd\H{o}s-Simonovits conjecture. Specifically, for $r \geq 4$, we demonstrate that
$$T(r, K^r_{r+1}) \geq \left(1-\frac{1}{r-1} + \frac{c_r}{n^{1/(r-2)}}\right) \frac{n^r}{r!},$$
where $c_r > 0$ is a constant dependent solely on $r$. This result improves upon the previously best-known bound of $\left(1-\frac{1}{r-1}+ \frac{c'_r}{n^{1/(r-3/2)}}\right) \frac{n^r}{r!}$, which was derived from the construction by \citet{gluskin2013improvement}. Furthermore, our finding partially addresses a question posed by \citet{clifton2018turan}. The proof advances the methodology introduced by \citet{clifton2018turan} and incorporates a refined analysis of the associated linear programming problem. Additionally, we conjecture that the exponent $1/(r-2)$ in our lower bound is optimal. Finally, we present an upper bound featuring the same exponent, thereby confirming that the order of magnitude for the leading term of $T(r, K^r_{r+1})$ remains unchanged. This achievement relies on a novel extension of the generalized Rayleigh monotonicity principle to $r$-uniform hypergraphs, a contribution of independent significance. \textbf{Mathematics Subject Classification (2010):} 05C35, 05C60, 05D99, 90C26. \textbf{Keywords:} Tur\'an number, Tur\'an hypergraph, Tur\'an density, uniform hypergraph, matching, KKT complementarity conditions, monotonicity principle.

This problem is equivalent to determining the intersection of the null space of $A$ with the $\R$-minimizing element in $\range(A)$. We introduce a new iterative algorithm that converges globally to this solution for any initial point. The method is derived from a general approach for identifying the intersection of two closed subspaces, specialized here to the case where one subspace is the range of $A$ and the other is the null space of $A^T$. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing that the iterates remain within $\range(A)$, ensuring convergence to the desired solution rather than just the minimum norm solution. These conditions are satisfied precisely when $A$ is irreducible. Additionally, we demonstrate that under these conditions, the proposed method yields a solution distinct from that of the regularized system $(A^TA+\mu I)x=b$, which is the standard approach for $\R$-minimization. Finally, we present numerical examples illustrating the method's performance. This research was motivated by the need to compute the set $\mathcal{M}$ of minimum norm solutions to the inverse problem $L\phi=f$ in radiative transfer theory, where $L$ is reducible. In that context, $\mathcal{M}$ corresponds to the intersection of the range of $L$ and the null space of $L^T$. We show that when $L$ is irreducible, the regularized system fails to yield a solution in $\range(L)$, whereas our method successfully does. This enables the computation of a solution to the inverse problem that is not the minimum norm solution, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the resulting estimates. \textbf{AMS(MOS) Subject Classification}: 15A09, 15A24, 15A23, 65F10, 65F30, 92C40. \textbf{Key Words}: Range, Irreducible matrix, minimum norm solution, regularized system, intersection of subspaces, iterative method.

for investigating quantum gravity phenomena and establishing a rigorous background-independent formalism. This study examines two specific models: Weyl gravity, which utilizes a conformally invariant theory based on the Weyl tensor, and the Cotton connection, a torsion-based theory applicable in three dimensions. Our primary objective is to derive the corresponding Hamiltonian systems and analyze their asymptotic dynamics. We demonstrate that in the low-energy regime, both theories yield identical solutions. Furthermore, at the semi-classical level, we establish that these system solutions correspond to conformal field theory solutions, thereby extending the solutions previously obtained for Einstein's general relativity. This finding offers a robust foundation for constructing a consistent and rigorous theory of conformal gravity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of the high-energy behavior of these systems. Finally, we investigate the implications of these solutions for the cosmological evolution of the universe. We find that the low-energy asymptotic solutions in both Weyl and Cotton gravity resemble those of standard general relativity, yet they predict a universe with a non-zero, negative cosmological constant. This results in a de Sitter universe characterized by accelerated expansion, contrasting with the open universe scenario derived from Einstein's original general relativity. These findings offer a novel perspective on the low-energy cosmological behavior of the universe. Furthermore, we observe that the high-energy asymptotic solutions exhibit a universal behavior, independent of the specific gravitational theory under consideration. This behavior is described by a universal function that remains invariant across different theories. Consequently, this universality provides a consistent framework for unifying various theories of gravity. We also show that this behavior is compatible with the high-energy asymptotic solutions of standard general relativity. Finally, we demonstrate that this behavior aligns with the solutions of conformal field theory in the semi-classical limit. Collectively, these results offer a consistent description of the universe's behavior across all energy scales within the context of conformal gravity. networks, this paper introduces a new distributed protocol designed to ensure fair and efficient medium access. Specifically, we formulate a stochastic dynamic programming model that accounts for time-varying user data buffers and backoff mechanisms. Leveraging this model, we define a policy termed the Buffer-Aware (BA) policy, which utilizes buffer state information to adjust transmission probabilities across varying network conditions. However, since users in practical scenarios cannot observe each other's buffer states, we develop the Buffered-Distributed (BD) policy, which relies only on individual user buffer states and achieves near-optimal performance compared to the BA policy. Furthermore, we propose the Buffered-Distributed-Random (BD-R) policy, which incorporates randomization to further enhance performance. Extensive simulations demonstrate that BD and BD-R users achieve significantly superior throughput and fairness (measured by Jain's fairness index) across diverse settings, including variations in the number of users, packet arrival rates, and minimum backoff slots. These results indicate that buffer-awareness is essential for improving both throughput and fairness, and that utilizing distributed buffer state information yields near-optimal outcomes. Additionally, our findings suggest that integrating buffer state knowledge into the existing IEEE 802.11 protocol could substantially improve WiFi network performance. Finally, we outline the specific modifications required to implement the BD and BD-R protocols within the IEEE 802.11 framework. To the best of our knowledge, this work offers the most comprehensive investigation into buffer-aware medium access for home WiFi to date.
